Technical Validation: Keepit 
Keepit 
The Keepit platform was designed to offer independent and dedicated cloud-native data protection for business-
critical SaaS workloads. This platform supports the most common SaaS applications, including Microsoft 365, 
Google Workspace, Salesforce, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Azure DevOps, Microsoft Power Platform, Microsoft 
Dynamics 365, and Zendesk (see Figure 2). Keepit is currently working to expand coverage to additional 
productivity, collaboration, project management, and other business-critical SaaS applications. 
Figure 2. Keepit Platform 
 
 
 
Source: Enterprise Strategy Group, now part of Omdia 
The Keepit platform has been purpose-built to focus on SaaS data backup and recovery with security and cost-
effectiveness in mind. Unlike conventional backup solutions built on the public cloud, Keepit’s vendor-independent 
cloud is physically hosted in Equinix data centers in multiple regions throughout the world, isolating backup data 
from any service-disrupting event experienced by the cloud service provider in which the SaaS application 
operates. Keepit owns the security of these data centers. They are not shared, and Keepit does not use 
subcontractors. To enhance performance and security of data protection operations, Keepit data centers maintain 
direct network connections with SaaS providers. 
While the platform uses commodity servers (owned and operated by Keepit), the software technology stack is 
proprietary—OS, Web server, log server, indexing, and cataloguing functions. By not using any public cloud or third-
party technology services within the stack, Keepit can reduce the attack surface and, more importantly, the risk of 
service-impacting issues originating outside of Keepit. 
Keepit has also been designed to provide fast backup and recovery times. All backup data is stored on a large fleet 
of spinning disk, which provides both high throughput for sequential I/O and high simultaneous I/O operations per 
second (IOPS) at lower cost than flash. Additionally, all data is hot; organizations do not need to tier data for backup 
and recovery purposes.

5 
Technical Validation: Keepit 
To ensure that organizations can maintain the integrity of their backup data and enable clean restores, the Keepit 
platform employs blockchain technology—specifically, a Merkle tree structure—to verify data integrity. With the 
Merkle tree, Keepit automatically verifies each data block as it is read or written. Because each block has its own 
embedded cryptographic signature, the data is verified automatically; no one can alter or change the data in any 
backup. Deduplication is automatic because the Merkel tree eliminates writing the same data multiple times. 
The performance and cost efficiencies delivered by its platform architecture enable Keepit to charge a flat fee per 
seat, with unlimited storage and transmission, as opposed to charging according to the volume of backup data. 
Since it owns and develops the technology stack, Keepit can offer this flat fee rather than passing on costs of third 
parties incorporated into the platform. With this flat fee, organizations will not incur additional storage costs should 
the amount of backup data increase or transfer fees. Organizations also do not have to worry about costs for storing 
duplicate data, as deduplication is automatically provided. Costs for tiering data are also eliminated, as all data is 
hot. 
Keepit is also compliant in handling and securing data across industries, as the company has earned multiple 
certifications, such as HIPAA, NIST, and PCI, and is ISO 27001 certified for both its data centers and processes. 
Enterprise Strategy Group Technical Validation  
Enterprise Strategy Group validated how organizations can benefit from using the Keepit platform to back up and 
restore their SaaS application data. We focused on how Keepit simplifies backup of SaaS application data, access 
to backup data (without risking overwrites or accidental deletion), restoration, and maintenance of backup history. 
Simplifying the Backup Process 
Due to varying architectures and infrastructures used by cloud service providers to deliver their SaaS applications, 
backup processes can differ. Many organizations wrongly believe that because their data and applications are now 
delivered as a service, they will be automatically backed up and recovered. The reality is that this is just not the 
case. While the SaaS provider will protect its own infrastructure and data for the purposes of running its service, 
customer satisfaction, and compliance, etc., the end-user organization is always responsible for its data. Legacy 
tools and on-premises capabilities were not designed to offer data protection across on-premises and SaaS 
workloads, which can hinder their ability to recover quickly, easily, and effectively at a manageable cost. 
With Keepit, organizations experience a consistent workflow for backing up data, regardless of the application. 
Keepit has been designed to greatly simplify backup operations, saving both time and operational expenses.

Enterprise Strategy Group navigated to the Keepit UI and observed how to set up a connector, a key component in 
initiating the backup process for any supported SaaS application. These connectors are supported by the direct 
network connections Keepit maintains with supported SaaS providers. We began by adding a Microsoft 365 
connector (see Figure 3).

Accessing Data Without Incurring Risk 
When needing to access specific data (e.g., a single email or document), guardrails are ideally in place to prevent 
accidental changes or deletions or opening potential doors for cyberattacks. With Keepit, data access can be 
completed without the need to search through all data associated with a specific application. Organizations can also 
access data without rehydration, as there is no tiering or fragmentation of data when backed up with Keepit.

Why This Matters 
Public SaaS applications continue to become more pervasive in corporate environments. In fact, Enterprise 
Strategy Group research found that 56% of organizations will increase their investment in public SaaS 
applications.2 Yet, the continued adoption of public SaaS highlights the challenges that organizations face in 
backing up the applications’ data in light of the shared responsibility model. Building and configuring in-house 
backup solutions for individual SaaS applications can be too difficult and time-consuming to justify 
undertaking such efforts. 
Enterprise Strategy Group validated that Keepit can simplify the backup process for a wide variety of public 
SaaS applications available in the market. We observed how this platform standardizes the workflow for 
backing up a public SaaS application, regardless of the cloud service provider or its underlying 
infrastructures. Time and effort for setting up the backup process is drastically reduced when compared to 
building out backup solutions for individual applications.

Technical Validation: Keepit 
Figure 7. Viewing Backup Data of Microsoft OneDrive 
 
 
Source: Enterprise Strategy Group, now part of Omdia 
Keepit’s approach for access eliminated the need to directly interact with the data, thus preserving its integrity and 
security. The approach can also help to reduce the time and effort of exactly locating any data to be viewed and 
restored when desired. With this view-only access, specific data from the supported public SaaS applications could 
be recovered without needing to search through or restore all application data. 
 
 
 
Why This Matters 
Circumstances may warrant accessing a select data set residing within all backup data of a specific 
application. With traditional backup solutions, locating that data will most likely involve searching through all 
backup data and/or rehydrating data (if data has been tiered). This easily results in wasting time, effort, and, 
subsequently, money.    
Enterprise Strategy Group validated that the Keepit platform enables data access without the need to touch 
the actual backup data. We observed how organizations can search for select items without the need to 
touch the actual data. By using public URLs that point to the selected data, organizations can then view, 
download, or print. This approach to accessing data also helps with quickly recovering data without restoring 
entire backups.

Technical Validation: Keepit 
Ensuring Restoration of Clean Data 
Restoring data from backup should ideally be done with clean data. With Keepit, the process for backing up data 
ensures that data integrity is preserved in all immutable snapshots. 
Enterprise Strategy Group Analysis

“AzureAD” connector. After selecting “Policies,” we chose to view backup history associated with the policy named 
“Definition” (see Figure 8). For each backup, such as the one captured on May 6 at 5:20:49 PM, we could see how

provenance, which is especially useful for audit and governance purposes.

Given how Keepit established data provenance, Enterprise Strategy Group noted how the platform assures

Why This Matters 
While organizations ideally want data restoration times to be as low as possible, any restoration is not 
successful if the backup data is not clean. Maintaining data integrity in backups is key in successfully 
restoring data and enabling normal business operations to continue. 
Enterprise Strategy Group validated that Keepit establishes data provenance throughout all created backups. 
We viewed how organizations can monitor and track changes made in data backups of any supported SaaS

that all created backups contain clean data, enabling effective data restoration as well as supporting audit 
and governance activities.

Conclusion 
Organizations face a wide variety of reasons that warrant data recovery, including cybersecurity events, system 
failure, malicious deletion, or accidental deletion.3 However, when it comes to public SaaS applications, 
organizations must remain aware of the shared responsibility model, which assigns the responsibility of backing up 
the application’s data to the customer. While organizations have the option to build data protection solutions, the 
drawback is having to tailor those solutions to each public SaaS application used, which might not be the best use 
of the limited time and resources they struggle to manage wisely. 
To simplify how organizations can protect the data of widely used public SaaS applications, organizations can opt to 
use Keepit. This cloud-native data protection platform has been designed for commonly used applications such as 
Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and Salesforce. With Keepit’s vendor-independent cloud, organizations have 
secure and automated backup with easy recovery. The underlying platform architecture—use of commodity servers 
and spinning disk, proprietary software technology stack, no tiering of backup data—enables Keepit to offer a 
powerful combination: flat pricing with unlimited storage and no data transfer fees and instant availability to data 
when recovery is needed.  
Throughout our evaluation, Enterprise Strategy Group validated that Keepit can help organizations to: 
• 
Simplify backups by offering a consistent workflow across all supported SaaS applications. 
• 
Access and recover specific data while maintaining data integrity and security. 
• 
Facilitate quick restoration with assurances that data is clean, thus resuming normal operations without 
incident. 
Organizations continue to expand their use of public SaaS applications to support a number of everyday business 
operations. Protecting the data of these SaaS applications then becomes critical so that business continues without 
incident. If your organization is looking for a secure, integrated, and flexible end-to-end SaaS data protection 
solution that is both simple to use and cost-effective, Enterprise Strategy Group recommends you seriously 
consider the Keepit SaaS data protection platform. Visit Keepit to learn more.

Future-proof isn’t a buzzword; it’s a design choice. 
Many companies are adopting AI because of pressure, hype, or fear of falling behind. Organizations tend 
to underestimate the cost of AI, the planning required, and the potential for unintended consequences 
when AI is allowed to act at scale. At the same time, the opposite challenge arises when people within 
the organization adopt AI whether the company is ready or not. If leadership is not intentional in providing 
approved tools, thinking through policies, and designing guardrails, shadow AI will fill the gap.
In a recent Keepit webinar, a panel of experts outlined critical risk areas IT and business leaders must address 
when developing AI capabilities. Read on for the key takeaways below.
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved.

risk exponentially.

a vendor’s AI usage may introduce compliance, 
privacy, or operational risk.
Data exposure and integrity risk
Because SaaS tools are highly connected, AI may 
access more data than intended, increasing to 
leakage or corruption risk.
Agentic AI risk 
Autonomous agents can act across systems, 
creating major risk if permissions, oversight, or 
rollback controls are weak.

When organizations do not provide sanctioned

Data loss scenarios in SaaS applications are multifold, from mistaken deletion, to misconfiguration,

Keepit is intelligently built to eliminate the burden and simplify processes for data recovery. It saves

our capabilities support fast and intelligent recovery, regardless of the data loss scenario.

Keepit’s solution
Access to data is a critical element when you need to recover. Common SaaS storage models use data 
tiering as a way to reduce storage costs. As a consequence, you’ll face hydration periods that delay 
recovery and unexpected retrieval costs when you need your data most.
The challenge: Limited access to data

a mishap at your cloud provider, or the most common cause of data loss — human error and 
misconfiguration — it’s often hard to determine just how much data has been lost. With limited insight, 
time needed to recover increases.
The challenge: Limited insight into data loss
Keepit’s data monitoring and anomaly detection capabilities help you identify possible issues early on for 
investigation and remediation. 
Full insight into what’s missing and what’s changed
When restoring data, the integrity of the data is a critical requirement. You need to be confident 
that any recovered data is accurate, complete, and free of malware. 
The challenge: Verifying the integrity of data
Keepit ensures data integrity for confident recovery. Keepit has been purposefully built to be tamper 
proof, offering a guarantee that data stays immutable. The application uses a Merkle Tree architecture 
which makes any low-level tampering impossible.

Evolving cyberthreats, rapidly shifting attacker tactics, and 
increasingly complex digital environments: Is your security 
strategy keeping up?
The past year has brought a wave of high-impact incidents — from 
sophisticated identity-driven attacks to supply chain infiltration and 
AI-augmented threats — that pushed organizations to rethink their 
cybersecurity posture.  Yet many teams still underestimate how quickly the 
threat landscape is accelerating. This was the key focus of a recent Keepit 
webinar, where Kim Larsen, CISO at Keepit, Paul Robichaux, senior director 
of product management at Keepit and Microsoft MVP, and Trent Widtfeldt, 
chief of engineering at Technologent, discussed significant cybersecurity 
trends as well as resilience lessons learned.
From AI-powered attacks and shadow AI to hybrid threats and cloud 
dependency, one theme was clear: Hope is not a strategy. Read the key 
takeaways for actionable strategies to make your security posture more 
resilient in 2026 and beyond. 
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved.
Key takeaways
The key takeaways
The complexity and power of cyberattacks is increasing — and so is accessibility. Capabilities once 
limited to nation-state actors are now within reach of individual attackers. AI is increasingly being used 
for attack planning, and the barrier to entry is falling. Your defenses must level up for a threat that is 
more automated than ever. 
Most shadow IT isn’t malicious — it’s employees trying to work faster. But AI often stores or transforms 
sensitive data, operates without governance, and exposes your organization to legal, ethical, and 
regulatory risk. The real risk is the speed gap: Adoption is happening faster than governance is being 
applied.
AI-powered attacks are accelerating 
Shadow AI is today’s silent risk
Is your cybersecurity strategy
ready for the challenge ahead?
AI introduces a new governance challenge. Frameworks like TRiSM emphasize transparency, 
continuous model monitoring, clear ownership and oversight, and embedded compliance controls. 
You can never eliminate AI risk fully, but you can make it manageable. Build guardrails before scaling 
adoption.
Governance needs to catch up

•	
Categorize, assess, and reduce risk 
•	
Establish a center of excellence within your 
organization and be clear on what resources 
and people you need 
•	
Plan and prioritize recovery of data and systems 
•	
Future-proof your architecture: Demand true 
immutability from your data protection vendor 
and physically/logically isolate your backups 
from your production data  
•	
Test restores regularly and run exercises and 
simulations with your team 
Organizations that will succeed in 2026 are not 
those that hope to avoid disruption but those 
that assume disruption, prepare for the worst, 
and practice recovery regularly. In a world of 
accelerating automation and converging threats, 
hope is not a strategy. Mapping relevant risks, 
preparing for them, and testing your contingency 
plans is.

Leading SaaS data security

cloud to safeguard essential business applications, boost cyber resilience, and future-proof data protection.

Threats no longer live in a single domain. We are seeing pivots from on-prem to cloud and vice 
versa, infrastructure sabotage, power failures, and regional disruptions, as well as natural disasters 
intersecting with digital dependency. The question is no longer if disruption happens — but whether 
your architecture and processes can withstand it.
In 2025, organizations experienced major SaaS outages, leaving organizations without access to 
critical systems and considerable downtime. True resilience requires independent backup outside 
the production ecosystem, clear prioritization of critical systems, and tested disaster recovery plans, 
including offline scenarios.
Security isn’t just about technology, it’s about working with your people as well as establishing 
processes. Effective organizations assume breach, run tabletop exercises and simulations, define 
recovery priorities, and align leadership on what matters most before incidents occur. Resilience is 
never a one-person job, but a unified cross-team effort.

1. Introduction 
This document serves as a guide to be used by Distributors, MSP Aggregators, and Partners, to 
understand the delivery of Keepit’s dedicated SaaS data protection solutions on a consumption 
model. Keepit offers a variety of scalable options to suit your customers’ needs. To understand 
Keepit’s terms for the service’s delivery, please refer to Keepit Terms of Service. 
2. Definitions 
Consumption Model 
On a consumption model all customers are paying for what they use of each backed up workload on a 
rolling monthly billing period 
Billing Period 
The default Keepit measuring period starts from the 20th of the month to the 20th of the following 
month. The monthly seat count will be based on the highest daily count of any workload in the billing 
period 
Account 
“Account” means a unique user identification name and password assigned to the Customer to enable 
an admin account in connection with the provision of the Services on the Keepit platform. 
Seat 
“Seat” is the metric Keepit used to measure the customer’s consumption of our services, and it also 
represents the customer’s entitlement to use the Services.  
Find additional definitions in Keepit Terms of Service.

SharePoint and Groups & Teams Fair-Usage Clause 
Keepit's Microsoft 365 backup solution provides comprehensive 
coverage for SharePoint, Groups, and Teams, even though the Seats 
count is based solely on users backed up in Exchange and OneDrive. 
To maintain optimal performance and service quality for all customers, 
the backup of SharePoint and Groups & Teams is governed by the 
following Fair Usage Clause. 
The number of users backed up in SharePoint and Groups & Teams is 
limited to four times (4x) the number of Seats backed up in Exchange 
and Mailboxes. If this ratio is exceeded and not corrected within 30 
days of notification from Keepit, Keepit reserves the right to charge 
additional Fees in accordance with the Terms of Service.

5. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) 
What happens if I backup a shared mailbox in Office 365?  
The backup of your Microsoft 365 Shared Mailbox, which has a Microsoft license associated to it, is 
counted as a seat within your Keepit subscription both for Keepit for Microsoft 365 and Keepit for 
Entra ID services. You can select and deselect a shared mailbox for backup in the configuration 
window of Keepit at any time. To learn how to do it, please refer to the Backup shared mailbox article 
on the Keepit Help Center.  
How can I exclude specific data areas from my Microsoft 365 backup? 
When you add a new Microsoft 365 connector, all data areas will be selected by default for your 
backup. You can also exclude data areas in your backup configuration.   
Why is my M365 seat count and Entra ID seat count not similar? 
The Entra ID connector calculates seat allocation based on users backed up within Entra ID. Seats 
are assigned to all users who hold either Microsoft 365 licenses or Entra ID–specific paid licenses. 
The Entra ID backup process counts all users included in the score of the Entra ID backup 
configuration settings. Consequently, if your Microsoft 365 connector backup configuration excludes 
certain users, the Entra ID seat count may exceed the Microsoft 365 seat count, as the Entra ID 
connector backs up and assigns seats to a broader user population. 
My contract mentions Active Users. Is this the same as Seats? 
Active Users was the term we previously used at Keepit to describe how we measure customer’s 
consumption of our services. To adapt to recent changes made by Microsoft in their licensing

About Keepit – The market leader in cloud backup and recovery, Keepit is headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark, with offices and 
data centers in the US and globally. 
 
8
structure, we are now using the term seats which is inclusive of active users and items (see definition 
in section 2 of this document).  
If your contract mentions Active Users, it is only because it was written prior to 2022. This has no 
impact on your contract and your agreed entitlement with Keepit. 
What if we have previous Office 365 users returning? 
You can recover a deleted Microsoft 365 user by using the Keepit Restore Wizard and importing the 
data back to the user from an appropriate snapshot.  
Learn more by reading our Recover a deleted Microsoft 365 user Help Center article.

As a company dedicated to keeping business-critical SaaS data safe and always available, 
no matter the incident, Keepit occupies a unique vantage point in the global data pro-
tection landscape. Every day, our platform processes millions of real‑world backup and 
restore operations across customers, regions, and SaaS applications. This gives us direct 
insight into how organizations actually protect, access, and recover their SaaS data — not 
how they intend to, or how they believe they do.
The Keepit Annual Data Report is built on that operational reality. It’s based on aggregated 
and anonymized  behavioral data drawn from our production backup environment, reflect-
ing backup and recovery activity across all active Keepit data center regions: Denmark, 
Germany, Switzerland, UK, Australia, Canada, and USA. At no point does the analysis rely on 
surveys, self‑reported behavior, or individual customer cases. Instead, it examines observ-
able patterns: how often data is backed up, how frequently restores occur, what types of 
recovery actions are initiated, and how backup systems behave under everyday — as well 
as unusual — conditions.
We believe this perspective is relevant well beyond Keepit’s customer base. Backup and 
recovery are often discussed in abstract terms — policies, architectures, or compliance 
requirements — while the day‑to‑day mechanics of data recovery remain poorly under-
stood. By focusing on what actually happens when organizations restore data, this report 
aims to ground those discussions in evidence.
Our goal is not to prescribe best practices or rank maturity, but to contribute transparency 
to an area that is foundational to digital resilience. By sharing population‑level insights de-
rived from real backup and recovery activity, we hope this report helps IT leaders, security 
professionals, and decision‑makers better understand the operational realities behind 
data protection — and make more informed choices as a result.
I hope you enjoy reading it.
Jakob Østergaard
Chief Technology Officer
Keepit
Introduction

Methodology
Data sources and scope
This report is based on aggregated and anonymized query results derived from Keepit’s production backup 
environment between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2025. In a few cases where explicitly stated, we 
included data for 2024 as well. The dataset reflects backup and restore activity across Keepit customers 
and includes data from all active data center regions: Denmark, Germany, Switzerland, United Kingdom, 
Canada, USA, and Australia. The analysis focuses on population‑level patterns and trends rather than orga-
nization‑specific behavior. At no point were individual customers, users, or datasets identifiable within the 
analytical process.
Data extraction and anonymization
To ensure strict separation between operational systems and analytical work, the dataset was extracted 
internally and anonymized prior to analysis. Data preparation was conducted by designated internal stake-
holders, who transferred the anonymized dataset to a dedicated server environment intended exclusively 
for analytical purposes. This approach ensured that analysts operated only on de‑risked data and had no 
access to live systems or customer‑identifiable information.
Data preparation and indexing
Before analysis commenced, the anonymized dataset was ingested and indexed to support efficient que-
rying and aggregation. Aggregated tables were created to enable analysis at scale while minimizing reli-
ance on granular operational records. This preparation improved query performance, ensured consistency 
across analytical outputs, and reduced the risk of exposing sensitive operational detail while preserving 
analytical validity.
Analytical approach
The analysis examined structural characteristics and recurring patterns related to backup and restore activ-
ity, including backup volumes, restore frequency and size, failure occurrences, change activity, and access 
behavior. Queries were executed against the aggregated dataset to surface distributions and trends ob-
servable across the full dataset. Results were interpreted at an aggregate level suitable for external report-
ing, with emphasis on comparability and clarity.
Validation and analytical review
Analytical outputs were reviewed iteratively to assess internal consistency, validate assumptions, and de-
termine relevance for publication. Findings were discussed between internal stakeholders and the external 
analysts to ensure that interpretations were supported by the data and that methodological constraints 
were appropriately reflected. Results that were insufficiently robust, overly granular, or ambiguous were 
excluded or further refined prior to inclusion.
Reporting and synthesis
Final results were synthesized and contextualized for reporting by the report author, with validation input 
from the external analyst. All findings are presented in aggregated form and are intended to illustrate 
general trends and behaviors across the dataset rather than precise measurements of individual customer 
environments.
Methodological limitations
The findings presented in this report are subject to several limitations. The use of anonymized and aggre-
gated data restricts the ability to account for contextual variables such as organizational size, industry, or 
IT maturity. The analysis reflects the structure and availability of operational data at the time of extraction; 
changes to underlying data models may affect comparability over time. In addition, aggregation may ob-
scure low‑frequency or edge‑case events that could be significant at an individual organizational level. 
These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results.

Chapter 1
Restore operations and job type
This chapter examines restore operations in practice. It analyzes how and when admini­
strators restore data, preferred recovery methods, and variations across time, regions, 
and business segments, offering insight into real-world recovery behavior and operation­
al priorities.
Job types	
	

 
By far the most common restore action is the “single file download” (90%).
Single file downloads are possible as an administrator using the user interface or as an end user with a 
“shared link” shared by an administrator. However, the number of such shared links created are insignificant 
compared to the number of downloads, and therefore the download numbers we observe are overwhelm-
ingly the result of administrator driven restore operations.
The second most common user-initiated job type is “bulk restore” (5%), third comes “zip download” (4%), 
and least common is “PST download” (1%).

What does that indicate?
The fact that the “single file download” is the most 
common restore action indicates that simple data 
loss incidents are the most common, and that ad-
ministrators appreciate the ability to do a simple, 
immediate recovery, rather than engage in more 
comprehensive restore operations.
Overall, across both regions and segments, “bulk 
restore” is the second most popular — an indication 
that when a single file download does not suffice, 
administrators prefer to put data back into its orig-
inal environment and repopulate live systems with 
backed-up data so users can pick up where they left 
off. 
As a close third comes downloading folders of doc-
uments (zip), while downloading entire mailboxes 
(PST) is not popular. The implication is that a zip file 
is immediately useful on the computer to which it’s 
downloaded, whereas a PST file needs to go through 
a PST import workflow through a mail client.

restore into the old destination where the files are missing. Restore jobs only overwrite data in 7% of cases.

months for restore operations.

Initiated restores by weekday and time of day
Weekdays
Restores are initiated seven days a week, but they follow the work week and are spread out evenly from 
Monday through Friday. While there are restores seven days a week, the majority of restore jobs (90%) are 
initiated Monday through Friday, with only a smaller part happening on weekends (10%).
The exception is the US, where the weekend sees 20% of initiated restores.
Other observations are that in the UK and Canada, there is more activity on Sundays (1.98% and 5.18% re-
spectively) than on Saturdays (0.79% and 1.98 respectively). 
And in Switzerland, there is almost no activity on Sundays (0.4%).

Time of day
Companies initiate restores 24/7, but as applies to the weekdays, the number of jobs are significantly higher

of the restores in SMB, 89.5% of restores in commercial, and 88.2% of the restores in enterprise.

What does that indicate?
The business segments follow the overall trends of restore versus downloads. The only surprise is the share

it’s sufficient for the job at hand. Larger and more mature organizations use single file download slightly less 
often than the smaller organizations, but the difference is miniscule (from 88.2% in enterprise to 91.7% in 
SMB).

Chapter 2
Data set observations
This chapter examines structural characteristics of backed-up datasets. It analyzes back­
up size development, file and byte change ratios, and regional variation, highlighting how 
data grows, changes, and behaves over time across different environments.
Backup size
When an organization first starts using Keepit Backup and Recovery, the first backup of the entire dataset is 
a major one. In relative terms, if the initial backup is 100%, subsequent backups each pull an additional 2% 
of data each.
There are exceptions: occasional spikes for some customers. This is typically caused by major organiza-
tional changes — i.e., mergers, acquisitions, or other operations that add significant datasets to the existing 
backup.

What does that indicate?
This is a demonstration of the effectiveness of Keepit’s “always incremental” strategy: Once a dataset is 
stored, only new files and changes to the original files are added. The complete file is not stored every time 
it’s changed. By keeping the daily backup size small, ongoing backups are fast, minimizing risk of conges-
tion and impact of service outages.

the 42% new files, and only 32% of ingested bytes come from modifications to the 58% existing files.

Chapter 3
User behavior
This section examines how organizations use backup and recovery in practice, including 
how often data is restored, which datasets are accessed, and whether external events 
influence restore activity or testing behavior across organizations, applications, and 
company sizes.
At Keepit, we recommend that organizations regularly test that their backup works, and not only that, but 
that the organization is able to restore critical data to the business environments to ensure business con-
tinuity in the event of data loss or outage events. This is important for business continuity, compliance, and 
brand image.
What we hope to see in this data is that organizations run regular restores — once a year at the bare minimum. 
That would indicate that they perform regular testing.
Restores by organization size
We see a correlation between size of the organization and restore frequency: Small and medium-sized 
businesses (SMBs) are less likely to restore regularly (28% do), while 91% in the commercial segment and 
95% in the enterprise segment are actively conducting and testing restores.

What does that indicate?
The data suggests that restore activity increases with organizational size, which is a natural outcome of hav-
ing more dedicated IT resources, more complex environments, and more frequent operational change. It’s 
also encouraging that most commercial and enterprise organizations show regular restore activity, indicat-
ing that recovery is not just a theoretical capability but something that is exercised in practice.
At the same time, the figures point to an opportunity — especially in the SMB segment — to build more 
routine recovery readiness. Many smaller organizations may experience fewer high-impact incidents day to 
day, and they often operate with limited administrative capacity. In that context, restores can easily become 
an “as-needed” activity rather than a scheduled practice. Introducing lightweight, guided recovery exer-
cises (even simple, repeatable checks) can help SMBs increase confidence, shorten response time when 
incidents occur, and steadily raise operational maturity over time. 
It’s also worth noting that “restore testing” can take multiple forms. While full bulk restore jobs provide the 
strongest validation of end-to-end readiness, even simple file downloads can confirm data accessibility, 
validate that teams know where to find the right data, and reinforce familiarity with recovery tooling. Build-
ing maturity is therefore not only about frequency, but also about progressing from ad hoc retrieval toward 
more structured, guided recovery workflows.

Chapter 3: User behavior
Keepit Annual Data Report 2026  |  16

Restores by application/dataset categories
Keepit operates with two categories of applications:  “Productivity applications” and “identity applications.” 
Productivity applications hold the datasets that organizations use to process data and communicate in their 
day-to-day operations — e.g., Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce.
Identity applications manage the identities, access rights, rules, permissions, and policies that enable the 
productivity applications to function and comply with the organization’s data regulations — e.g., Microsoft 
Entra ID and Confluence’s Okta.
Because of the nature of identity application data and the way that our statistical material is collected, we’ll 
disregard single file downloads in the following analysis and only consider “real” bulk restore jobs as well as 
bulk downloads.
When we look at how often organizations restore the two categories, we see that, on average, productivity 
applications are restored four times as frequently as identity applications. 
In other words: For every four companies who run a yearly test on their productivity workload, only one of 
them (25%) will have run a test on their identity applications.

What does that indicate?
The difference in restore activity between productivity and identity applications suggests that many orga-
nizations are further along in operationalizing recovery for day-to-day collaboration and business systems 
than they are for identity applications. This is understandable: Productivity datasets are the most visible to 
end users, and restore needs often surface quickly when business content is missing or changed. 
Identity systems, however, have a distinct role in enabling access across the broader SaaS environment. 
Strengthening recovery readiness for identity applications can therefore be seen as the next step in SaaS 
data protection maturity — expanding recovery planning from “business content” to the “access layer” that 
makes business operations possible. As awareness and tooling evolve, guided recovery practices and clear 
runbooks can help make identity recovery testing more approachable and easier to include in regular oper-
ational routines.
Impact on restore activity by external event
To understand if external, high-profile events cause any changes in restore behavior, we looked into two 
events of 2024 and one event of 2025 that could have caused data loss or unavailability. These are events 
we expected would lead IT professionals to double-check their disaster readiness, whether or not their 
organizations were directly impacted by the events. 
We analyzed user behavior around these three events that caused worldwide outages and received exten-
sive media coverage in the IT media. What makes them interesting to analyze is the fact that they generated 
a lot of global  awareness, and that each outage came from a different technological origin. 
1.	 The solar flares of May 2024: solar activity affecting Earth’s magnetic environment.
2.	 The CrowdStrike incident of July 2024: a defective endpoint protection update that crashed Microsoft Windows 
systems.
3.	 The Microsoft outages of October 2025: an Azure control plane misconfiguration causing widespread outages on 
Microsoft 365, Entra ID, and more.
The result: None of these events prompted any change in user behavior. We do not see any sign of increase 
in activity to test that backups were working in the days and weeks following the event.

What does that indicate?
The data shows no measurable increase in restore testing activity following the outage events. One inter-
pretation is that organizations did not experience widespread, immediate restore needs as a direct result 
of these events — an encouraging sign that many environments remained operational despite external 
disruption.
More broadly, the results also suggest that “awareness moments” do not automatically translate into chang-
es in recovery routines. This highlights an opportunity: Organizations can use external events as structured 
triggers for guided recovery checks — short, repeatable validations that reinforce confidence without 
requiring large-scale, disruptive exercises. Over time, this kind of guided approach can help teams build 
steady recovery maturity rather than relying on reactive learning during high-pressure incidents.
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
Chapter 3: User behavior
Keepit Annual Data Report 2026  |  19

Conclusion
Recovery is the true test of backup
The data in this report points to a clear operational takeaway: Backup creates value when organizations 
can recover — confidently, correctly, and efficiently, whether the need is small and immediate or broad and 
time-critical. 
Restore activity is strong among larger organizations. In enterprise and commercial segments, most organi-
zations perform restores regularly, indicating that recovery is not only planned but exercised. This reflects a 
growing level of operational maturity: Many organizations are actively validating that they can regain access 
to data when it matters. 
The same patterns also highlight an important maturity opportunity in the SMB segment. A significant share 
of SMBs did not initiate restores during the year, and bulk restore activity is less common. From an SMB 
perspective, this can be explained by limited administrative bandwidth and the perception that backup is 
something you configure once and rarely touch. The practical implication is not that backup is ineffective, 
but that recovery confidence may be harder to establish without periodic, lightweight testing. Structured, 
guided recovery exercises can help smaller organizations build readiness gradually — without turning re-
covery into a complex project. 
The report also shows that restore behavior is dominated by single file downloads. This reflects real oper-
ational needs: Many incidents are granular, and retrieving a specific file is fast and convenient. At the same 
time, organizations benefit from ensuring they can also execute recovery workflows that scale — where 
larger datasets, multiple users, or entire environments must be restored. Developing proficiency in bulk 
restore is a key step in maturity, turning recovery from an improvised response into a repeatable capability. 
We also observe a consistent execution pattern in bulk restores: Administrators typically restore into a new 
destination, or where files are missing, and overwrite is comparatively rare. This suggests a cautious, risk-
aware approach — favoring clean recovery paths that minimize the chance of unintended changes. This is 
a healthy operational instinct, and it further supports the value of practicing guided restore workflows so 
teams can act quickly while maintaining control. 
Finally, the findings highlight a maturity gap between productivity and identity applications. Identity data is 
restored and tested less frequently than productivity data, even though identity services underpin access 
across many SaaS environments. As organizations expand their SaaS protection strategies, improving iden-
tity recovery readiness is a natural next step — supported by clearer procedures, better visibility, and guided 
recovery assistance. 
Keepit believes AI can help lower the barrier to doing recovery well. Guided recovery — enabled by MCP 
(Model Context Protocol) — opens the door to “asking for help” in the moment that matters. An MCP-en-
abled assistant can help identify unhealthy tenants or suspicious patterns in protected data and guide 
administrators through the right recovery steps, turning recovery into a manageable, repeatable process. 
Even with AI support, regular rehearsal remains valuable — because confidence in recovery is built through 
practice. 
If you would like to discuss what these findings mean for your environment — and how to strengthen maturity 
in bulk restore and guided recovery — please reach out to Keepit to learn more.
 /Jakob Østergaard

Glossary
Job types
Backup
When organizations perform or schedule backups of their data, storing data in the Keepit cloud.
Restore
A restore in Keepit means putting data back into its original environment — repopulating live 
systems with backed‑up data so users can continue working.  Typical use case: operational 
recovery, e.g., restoring a deleted email back into a user’s mailbox.
Bulk restore
A restore operation where more than one file is restored at once, as opposed to a single file 
download.
Single file download
When an administrator locates a single file in a backup set — via browsing or search — and 
downloads it directly through the web interface, either for themselves or to share with an end 
user.
Zip download
Downloading folders of documents as a compressed zip file — retrieving and exporting data 
rather than restoring it to a live system. Typical use case: audits, compliance, or manual review.
PST download
Downloading entire mailboxes as PST files. Typical use case: mailbox archiving, migration, or 
integration into PSBulk restore T‑based business support workflows.
Business segments
SMB*
Fewer than 1,000 seats
Commercial
1,000–5,000 seats
Enterprise
More than 5,000 seats
*Small and medium‑sized business
Dataset and backup terminology
Backup size
The total volume of data included in a backup at a given point in time.
File number
The total number of files included in a backup dataset.
Day One
The initial backup of a dataset when an organization first starts using Keepit, serving as the 
baseline for subsequent incremental backups.
New files
Files that did not previously exist in the backup dataset and are ingested for the first time.
Changed files
Existing files that have been modified since the previous backup and are therefore re‑ingested.
New bytes
The total volume of data ingested from files that are new to the backup dataset. New bytes 
represent the size contribution of files that did not previously exist in the dataset and are backed 
up for the first time.
Changed bytes
The total volume of data ingested as a result of changes to existing files. Changed bytes 
represent the size contribution of modifications made to files that already exist in the backup 
dataset.

When a breach hits, every second counts, and 
immutability is what keeps those seconds from 
turning into days of downtime.
It’s a tough environment out there where threat actors routinely bypass 
perimeter defenses. Adopting a breach-assumed mindset is no longer 
optional — it’s essential.
This was the key focus of a a recent Keepit webinar, where Paul Robichaux, 
Senior Director of Product Management at Keepit and Microsoft MVP, and 
Bart Binder, Red Team Manager at Keepit, discussed how isolation plus 
immutability stops any tampering of your backup in its tracks, and which 
design choices (short-lived tokens, ingest-time locks, separated planes) 
actually matter. Read the key takeaways to turn principles into practical 
steps that strengthen your SaaS backups and speed up recovery. 
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved.
Key takeaways
The key takeaways
Are you breach ready? 
Learn how immutability minimizes damage
The question isn’t whether immutability reduces 
breach impact; it demonstrably does. The real 
discussion is about which implementation you 
choose, because the type of immutability you 
choose changes your ability to quickly and 
completely recover.
In many instances, attackers attempt to purge 
logs and bulk-delete backups. In an example 
discussed, the chain broke only because the 
storage layer enforced WORM at ingest and delete 
calls were refused. Breaches only take minutes 
to compromise, but immutability can give teams 
critical days to respond.
Checksums and signatures are valuable to detect 
corruption, but preventing alteration in the first 
place is far stronger. Immutability should be your 
last line of defense when everything else (perimeter, 
credentials, controls) is failing.
Air-gapping has a modern form: Keep backups in 
an environment attackers can’t pivot into. Placing 
Microsoft 365 data in a vendor-independent cloud 
with no dependencies on Azure/AWS/GCP (and no 
shared credentials/replication paths) removes a 
rich attack surface. Replication helps with disasters, 
but it’s not true protection if an attacker can reach 
every replica. 
Immutability isn’t a debate — 
it’s a requirement 
Real-world kill chain = minutes 
to compromise
Tamper detection ≠ 
immutability
Isolation matters as much as 
immutability

Leading SaaS data security
Breach-ready actions for your 
organization: 
Demand true immutability (locked at ingest, 
hardware-anchored time, no-modify APIs). 
Physically/logically isolate backups from primary 
clouds and identities. 
Enforce short-lived tokens and conditional 
access. 
Separate control/storage planes; require dual 
control for destructive changes. 
Test restores frequently (including large-scale 
and identity/control-plane scenarios). 
Pair immutability with DLP/classification 
upstream and practiced incident response. 
Keepit’s storage design: Immutability 
by design
Keepit stores data in a Merkle tree object store 
with only two operations — read block and write 
block.There is no “modify block” API. Each version 
chains cryptographic hashes to prior blocks, 
delivering built-in dedupe, integrity verification, 
and tamper evidence.
Combined with an independent, vendor-neutral 
cloud, this yields practical air-gap properties in 
addition to provable immutability.

Storage flags that mark data “immutable” 
at the software layer can be undermined via 
misconfigurations, API abuse, or clock spoofing. 
Strong designs lock objects at ingest, anchor time 
in hardware (e.g., TPM), and prevent public APIs 
from ever reaching the storage plane. 
Immutable backups limit the ability to remove 
inadvertently stored sensitive content later. 
Mitigation should be earlier in the lifecycle: 
Data classification and data loss prevention in 
production will prevent unwanted data from being 
created or synced, rather than relying on post-hoc 
removal from backups. 
Token theft and reuse are fast-rising attack 
vectors. Keep token lifetimes as short as practical 
and layer conditional access. A stolen token that 
expires in an hour is dramatically less useful than one 
valid for a day. 
Immutability dramatically limits ransomware 
leverage and preserves your ability to restore, but 
it doesn’t replace zero trust, endpoint controls, IR 
processes, or business continuity planning. Recov-
ery speed still hinges on role-based access, guided 
restores, tested runbooks, and organizational 
readiness. 
“Checkbox immutability” is 
not enough 
Trade-offs are real — choose 
protection over perfection

blast radius

From threat to defense:
Ransomware and cyber insurance
Ransomware plagues security professionals — and, 
in turn, the companies that insure them — more 
than ever before. It’s now one of the most signif-
icant cybersecurity challenges, with 89% of en-
terprises identifying it as a top-five threat to their 
business. No longer limited to isolated incidents, 
ransomware has evolved into a booming global 
economy as attackers expand their capabilities 
and collaborate across networks.
This was a key focus of discussion during a recent 
Keepit webinar, where Kim Larsen, CISO at Keepit, 
engaged a panel of cybersecurity and IT experts to 
discuss trends in ransomware and how they affect 
an organization’s ability to secure cyber insurance 
today.
Actionable strategies to build resilience against the threat
© 2024 Keepit. All rights reserved.
•	 Ensure active monitoring and conduct regular vulnerability 
assessments to identify and mitigate potential entry points. 
•	 Focus on initial access points, as most breaches occur here. 
•	 Deploy compartmentalization strategies to contain threats 
and prevent lateral movement within systems. 
1. Proactive defense
•	 Develop a cybersecurity maturity framework that includes 
multi-factor authentication (MFA), Endpoint Detection 
and Response (EDR), privileged access management, and 
employee awareness training.
•	 Test incident response plans and conduct tabletop 
exercises regularly to ensure operational resilience. 
3. Insurability controls
•	 Store backups offsite and frequently check for corruption to 
maintain recovery readiness. 
•	 Implement robust detection systems to identify 
compromises before restoration is necessary. 
•	 Conduct regular restoration exercises, at least annually, to 
verify backup integrity. 
2. Comprehensive backup systems
•	 Shift to a “we are being attacked” mindset. Resilience, not 
just defense, is essential to maintaining operations during and 
after an attack. 
•	 Use established frameworks like NIST or ISO to create 
structured and measurable security policies. 
4. Resilience building
Read more about how one of our 
customers recovered from a cyber attack
Key takeaways

© 2024 Keepit. All rights reserved.
Cyber insurance has become a cornerstone of risk management, providing financial protection against 
cyberattacks. It complements proactive initiatives like incident response planning and data recovery 
processes, acting as a safety net against increasingly sophisticated threats.
However, securing coverage is not straightforward. As threats evolve, so do insurer requirements. Insurers 
now demand evidence of cybersecurity maturity, often rejecting applicants without critical safeguards 
such as MFA, monitoring, or access controls. Policies also require proof of implementation rather than mere 
declarations of compliance, underscoring the need for demonstrable cybersecurity practices.

Introduction
Data sits at the center of both the biggest risks and the biggest opportunities facing your organization. 
CISOs and CIOs are responsible for safeguarding data with robust protections while also ensuring it’s 
available — in the right forms, to the right people, at the right time — to power both day-to-day operations 
and innovation initiatives.
For a number of reasons — including an unpredictable geopolitical landscape, the market dominance 
of a handful of hyperscalers, stricter privacy regulations, and uptime/availability requirements — digital 
sovereignty has rapidly emerged as a strategic priority. And data sovereignty, a necessary element 
of digital sovereignty, is driving organizations to take a closer look at cloud architectures, vendor 
dependence, the supply chain and use of sub-processors, and compliance requirements.
At a glance, digital sovereignty may seem to fall squarely under the purview of CISOs and legal counsel; 
however, its significance to your organization is such that digital sovereignty is more accurately regarded 
as a business issue of the utmost importance.
The world is changing, and — like it or not — these 
changes are forcing CEOs and boards to make 
decisions that have profound consequences.
For Keepit, digital sovereignty isn’t a theoretical 
ideal — it’s a cornerstone of our philosophy and 
our technology.
For more than 20 years, we’ve provided 
dedicated data protection, putting organizations 
in control of their own SaaS data. We own and 
operate a vendor-independent cloud, with 
no-transfer guarantees, to protect critical data 
across platforms like Microsoft 365, Microsoft 
Entra ID, Salesforce, and Google Workspace.
For IT leaders, this means autonomy: knowing 
exactly where your data is, who is handling it, and 
how it is being protected — free from third-party 
influence.
In an era where political alliances change 
at the whim of mercurial leaders, creating 
and amplifying sovereignty risks, Keepit 
collaborates with our customers to implement 
best practices, stay ahead of emerging threats, 
and continuously improve data governance 
strategies.
This document is one outcome of those 
collaborative conversations.

What is data 
sovereignty?
01

Data sovereignty report  |  6
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
A key element of digital sovereignty
Sovereignty means autonomy; that is, freedom from external control.
Digital sovereignty encompasses (in fact, requires) control over digital infrastructure, including data, 
operations, and technology (Figure 1). It’s about an entity’s ability to manage and control its digital 
environment — the freedom to store and run workloads wherever desired, for whatever reason (e.g., 
performance, resilience, compliance, etc.) — ensuring autonomy in the cyber realm. Digital sovereignty 
mitigates the risks associated with foreign data control or influence and consequently is a strategic 
imperative for aligning with regulatory frameworks within geographic boundaries.
Data sovereignty refers to the legal and regulatory control that a country or region has over data generated 
or residing within its borders. It dictates how data can be used, who can access it, and which laws apply to 
its handling. Data sovereignty ensures that data is subject to the laws of the country of origin.
Key takeaways:
• Data sovereignty refers to the legal and regulatory control over data, and is of 
vital importance for most organizations working on digital sovereignty.
• Digital sovereignty is a broad concept encompassing control over digital 
infrastructure — including data, hardware, and software.
• Data residency, which refers to the physical (geographic) location 
of data, is a key aspect of digital sovereignty.
What is data sovereignty?

Common data forms
Some of the most common and sensitive forms of data are:
•	 Intellectual property including trade secrets, algorithms, business 
process details, source code, and customer lists
•	 Internal and external communications, including text or chat messages, emails, 
voice calls, and videoconference recordings and transcripts
•	 Employee, customer/client, and third-party service provider data including personally identifiable 
information (PII), personal health information (PHI), and payment card information (PCI)
•	 Operational telemetry and sensor data, such as security events and 
capacity, performance, or load distribution data
•	 Identity and access management (IAM) data, including keys, tokens, and credentials
For most organizations pursuing digital sovereignty, achieving data sovereignty is the largest challenge. 
There are a number of reasons why this is the case, including:
•	 Today’s organizations work with massive volumes of data.
•	 Data exists in a wide range of forms, many of which are subject to regulatory requirements pertaining to 
privacy and security.
•	 Modern IT environments include complex combinations of public and private clouds, software-as-a-service 
(SaaS) applications, and on-premises infrastructure — plus local storage on devices such as laptops and 
mobile phones.
•	 Data is very easy to move, and tends to move around a lot during its lifecycle (Figure 2).
•	 Where data is stored or processed, what paths it traverses when it’s moved or used, and which companies play 
a role in these activities are often opaque.

Data residency
Data sovereignty
Figure 3 – Data sovereignty, a requirement of digital sovereignty, 
is itself shaped by several factors
Data residency refers to the physical location(s) 
where data is stored, processed, or otherwise 
handled.
Data residency is a key aspect of data sovereignty, 
for the straightforward reason that data residency 
often determines data sovereignty. That is, where 
data is held or used strongly influences — or even 
entirely dictates — associated legal obligations.
Moreover, today’s IT environments and data flows 
can be so complex that accurately understanding 
data residency can itself present a significant 
challenge. For example, data may be collected in 
one country, processed by a third party in another 
country, stored in another country, and backed up in 
yet another country. The data in such a scenario can 
be considered to reside in four countries, with four 
associated sets of data sovereignty obligations.
It’s also important to note that data residency is 
distinct from (but related to) data localization, with 
the latter referring to a legal requirement that data 
stay where it was created (or acquired). Where data 
localization laws apply, the causal chain extends 
one step further back: Data localization determines 
data residency, which then determines data 
sovereignty.
However, data residency requirements need not 
come from data localization requirements — many 
data residency requirements come from an 
organization’s internal policies or contractual 
obligations (Figure 3).

Hyperscalers are companies that provide — with considerable flexibility and extreme scale — cloud 
computing resources including processing, memory, networking, and storage.
As organizations around the globe increasingly focus on core competencies, work with ever-expanding 
volumes of data, and explore data- and compute-intensive innovations, hyperscalers have emerged as a 
major foundation of much of the digital world.
However, by outsourcing much of what used to be done by in-house IT teams — including building, 
maintaining, and operating data centers or managing on-premises applications — organizations have 
collectively ceded tremendous control to a small number of international players. As a result of these 
Why data sovereignty 
matters
Key takeaways:
• Major reasons why data sovereignty is becoming a strategic imperative include a rapidly changing 
(and seemingly unpredictable) geopolitical landscape, dependence upon a handful of dominant 
hyperscalers, stricter privacy regulations, and availability and recovery requirements.
• Organizations routinely find themselves caught between foreign laws or regulations 
that compel data access (e.g., under the guise of national security interests) and local 
laws or regulations that demand data protection (e.g., to preserve privacy).
• Data sovereignty provides some degree of immunity against foreign laws and regulations, 
while also promising greater resilience in the face of hybrid warfare and supply chain 
threats, plus stronger compliance with availability and recovery obligations.

Data sovereignty report  |  11
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
decisions, organizations have (often unknowingly) traded technical complexity for legal complexity.
Geopolitics and hyperscaler dominance
Geopolitics and hyperscaler dominance bring data sovereignty to the forefront. 
As of November 2024, 97% of the cloud infrastructure and platform services market was dominated by US 
and Chinese hyperscalers:
Unfortunately, the global cloud market is not just about technology — increasingly, it’s about politics and 
control.
Dependency upon these few players leaves organizations worldwide vulnerable to political shifts and 
foreign legislation, and today’s organizations find themselves caught between:
•	
National security and law enforcement acts (e.g., the United States’ Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act or 
the CLOUD Act) that compel access to data, even if it resides in foreign datacenters
•	
Privacy regulations (e.g., the European Union’s General Data Protection Act or GDPR) that require organizations 
to prevent data from being accessed by, among others, foreign entities
As a concrete example of this challenging and shifting regulatory landscape, the EU’s landmark Schrems 
II ruling issued in July 20201 invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield framework, in part because of a 
determination that US laws2  had several shortcomings that impeded the protection of personal data and 
violated the GDPR.
Until its 2020 demise, the Privacy Shield codified an adequate level of protection against the personal data 
of EU citizens being accessed by the US government and its various agencies. Now, however, EU-based 
1 July 16, 2020: Case C-311/18 Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland and Maximillian Schrems

2 In particular: US Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) Section 702, Executive Order 12333, and Presidential Policy Directive 28

Data sovereignty report  |  12
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
organizations that conduct business in the US do so under a cloud of uncertainty, with no clear guidance as 
to how to continue such operations without running afoul of GDPR.
Privacy concerns reached new heights in June 2025 when, in testimony before the French Senate, Microsoft 
conceded that the CLOUD Act meant that the company could not guarantee that even data stored outside 
the US would be inaccessible to US authorities.
For organizations around the world, these revelations raised serious questions about the potential 
illegality of using cloud services operated by US companies to process or store data protected by privacy 
regulations, especially in the public sector and highly regulated industries such as healthcare and finance.
As just one of many examples available, shortly after the Schrems II ruling, France’s data regulator 
(Commission nationale de l’informatique et des libertés, or CNIL) recommended that French services 
handling health data avoid using US cloud providers.

Tellingly, the recommendations extend beyond not using US providers to process data: The CNIL went

business with US-based companies. As TechCrunch reported, “It’s not just about processing European 
data in Europe,” it’s “all about avoiding falling under US regulation and rulings.”
Digital sovereignty as a legal protection mechanism
In the face of such a dilemma (e.g., complying with US laws and violating local ones, or the opposite), digital 
sovereignty represents an organization’s ability to ensure autonomy and security in a constantly shifting 
political and cyber landscape.
In response to concerns from EU-based 
organizations, US-based hyperscalers 
have launched offerings (e.g., Microsoft 
365 EU Data Boundary, Amazon’s European 
Sovereign Cloud, Google’s Sovereign 
Controls) and run marketing campaigns 
oriented around data remaining in the EU.
However, the CLOUD Act makes it very clear 
that the location of data doesn’t matter, 
bypassing GDPR protections. 
For example, Article 48 of the GDPR states:
“Any judgment of a court or tribunal and 
any decision of an administrative authority 
of a third country requiring a controller or 
processor to transfer or disclose personal 
data may only be recognized or enforceable 
in any manner if based on an international 
agreement, such as a mutual legal assistance 
treaty, in force between the requesting third 
country and the Union or a Member State, 
without prejudice to other grounds for 
transfer pursuant to this Chapter.”
In contrast, the CLOUD Act:
•
Allows extraterritorial reach of US law
•
Does not require judicial review under EU 
legal systems
•
Does not provide adequate legal remedies 
for EU citizens
This clear contradiction is causing EU-based 
organizations with operations in the US to 
focus less on where data is stored and more 
on who controls the infrastructure in which 
data is stored.
Ultimately, if the infrastructure provider 
falls under US jurisdiction, then there is no 
guarantee of full GDPR compliance.
Infrastructure control comes  under scrutiny:
CLOUD Act versus GDPR
Why data sovereignty matters

Data sovereignty report  |  14
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Within individual nations or regulatory jurisdictions, sovereignty requirements are seen as a way to protect 
organizations — including the data they use and the workloads they run — from legal obligations imposed 
by external authorities.
In short, achieving digital sovereignty (and, by definition, data sovereignty) is expected to provide some 
degree of immunity from foreign laws or regulations that are at odds with local ones.
Secondary factors driving digital sovereignty initiatives
Looking beyond geopolitics, there are several 
other reasons why digital sovereignty is fast 
becoming a top-of-mind issue for organizations.
Supply chain risk
In recent years, organizations have taken a 
greater security-centric interest in their software 
supply chain due to a number of large-scale 
security incidents traced to compromised 
vendors and code repositories.
However, cloud infrastructure has largely 
avoided the same degree of scrutiny, despite an 
abundance of similar issues.
For instance, if a cloud identity provider (IdP) 
such as Microsoft or Okta suffers an outage 
due to an issue with the hyperscaler upon which 
they depend, then countless organizations will 
be rendered largely inoperable. (And while the 
impact may be smaller for most other SaaS 
outages, the general point still applies.)
“No problem,” leaders may think, “we have 
backups that will allow us to quickly recover and 
restore operations.”
Unfortunately, most SaaS backup solutions rely on the same hyperscalers as the SaaS providers. If a SaaS 
provider and backup provider use the same hyperscaler, then there’s a real problem: There’s no air gap. 
In certain scenarios (e.g., a natural disaster or other issue with a datacenter), geographic redundancy 
provides some measure of safety, but outages due to misconfigurations and errors have the potential to 
span multiple zones.
In contrast, sovereign backup providers provide a solution for fast, complete recovery by maintaining data 
availability, eliminating cross-border data replication through regional data centers, and minimizing cloud 
dependency via independent clouds.
Hybrid warfare
Today’s organizations operate in a very different global political and technological environment than their 
predecessors.
US Department of Defense 
Contractor
• Problem: A defense supplier needs to 
migrate HR and manufacturing systems 
to the cloud.
• Decision: They contract only providers 
offering “US-only sovereign regions” 
meeting DoD IL5/IL6 standards.
• Outcome: They pass DoD audit and 
secure contract extensions.

Why data sovereignty matters

Data sovereignty report  |  15
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Hybrid warfare blends cyberattacks, physical sabotage, disinformation, and economic coercion to 
disrupt or destabilize its targets, and the ease with which digital infrastructure can be targeted — coupled 
with the outsized impact caused by disruptions — puts hyperscalers and important SaaS applications 
squarely in the sights of adversaries.
For example,  an advisory issued by the FBI in August 2025 warned that Salt Typhoon — an advanced 
persistent threat actor believed to be operated by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) — targeted 
more than 600 organizations across 80 countries.
Consequently, a crisis, conflict, or even merely a test run (with plausible deniability) may render cloud-
based data inaccessible.
Data sovereignty provides added resilience against this new reality, making it essential for an 
organization’s risk management and long-term digital strategy.
Availability and recovery requirements
Increasingly, organizations are finding themselves beholden to requirements relating to availability and 
recovery and are recognizing that dependence upon third-party providers represents a risk.
While some of these obligations stem from contractual service level agreements (SLAs), many originate 
with regulatory bodies. For example, under the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)  and 
Network and Information Security 2 (NIS2) directive, organizations in critical sectors must prove that they 
can recover from information and communication technology (ICT) disruptions with minimal reliance on 
third-party connectivity.
Why data sovereignty matters

meant the insurer couldn’t prove who 
ultimately had access to data.
• Decision: They negotiated contracts 
specifying region, audit rights, and consent 
requirements for subcontractors.
• Outcome: BaFin approved the outsourcing, 
and the company gained a model framework 
for future cloud buys.

Unfortunately, the challenges outlined in the preceding sections are not merely theoretical; rather, they 
represent real risks and vulnerabilities for organizations with (or aspiring to have) international presence 
or customers.
In the emerging geopolitical and technological landscape, control, privacy, audit trails, and technology 
independence are not just aspirations — they are necessities for resilient digital operations.
Preparing your organization to not only survive in this environment, but to thrive, requires asking many 
simple questions and putting in the work to track down complex answers.
Questions IT leaders 
need to ask
Over-arching governance

□
How will we track progress towards digital 
sovereignty and, once achieved, how will we prove it 
(e.g., transparent monitoring of digital infrastructure, 
reports demonstrating independence, etc.)?
	
□
What data do we use (e.g., create/ingest, store, 
process/transform, archive)?
	
□
Where is this data stored?
	
□

policies?

hyperscalers?

□
Is our technology stack independent from and 
resilient against foreign influence?

 Supply chain and 
hardware sovereignty
Countries and regions are investing heavily in their own cloud data 
centers, AI factories, and supercomputing capacity so they are less 
dependent on foreign providers. For instance, in Europe, there are 
efforts to build “AI gigafactories” and to push for sovereign cloud 
offerings.
Hybrid architectures (mix of on-premises, edge, and cloud) may 
become more common as a way to balance regulatory compliance, 
performance, latency, and control — yes, we are seeing a movement 
back to being on-premises in certain scenarios.
Regulations — like the recently adopted EU Data Act, the EU AI Act, 
GDPR, and various national laws — are increasing requirements around 
data privacy, transparency of training data, risk assessments of AI 
models, etc.
Laws governing cross-border data flows, laws that grant data 
subjects certain rights (e.g., to know how data is used, to port their 
data, etc.), and restrictions on foreign (non-local) access to critical 
data (or infrastructure) are becoming more common around the globe.
A lot of digital and data sovereignty depends on physical infrastructure: 
chips, GPUs/TPUs, networking, servers, etc. Many countries are at risk 
because production of key hardware is concentrated in a few places 
(e.g., Taiwan, US, and China).
Moves to develop domestic or regional fabrication, design, 
and manufacturing capabilities are increasing. Concerns about 
dependencies (e.g., for rare earths, semiconductor tooling, etc.) are 
becoming strategic and political issues.
To best inform these activities, we believe organizations should monitor these 
major trends.
Eight trends to monitor in digital sovereignty

Data sovereignty report  |  32
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
4
	 Data sovereignty and 
memory/cognitive 
sovereignty
5
	
Geopolitical 
fragmentation/blocs
6
	
Ethics, trust,

7
	
Decentralization,

8
	
Environmental,

sustainability 
constraints
Beyond “just data location,” there is growing concern about who 
controls what memories or learned behavior an AI can use, how 
personalized assistants track and store user history, etc. This touches 
on “cognitive sovereignty” — ensuring that users or nations retain 
control over their narratives, personal profiles, etc.
There are increasingly prominent demands for AI systems to be 
designed such that memory is portable, transparent, auditable, and 
controllable.
The global AI ecosystem is increasingly splitting along geopolitical 
lines. For example, trade restrictions (export controls), sanction 
regimes, or simply policy divergence are pushing infrastructure, 
standards, and supply chains to align differently in, say, the US/EU 
bloc vs. China vs. others.
Regions want legal and technical standards (for privacy, transparency, 
and safety) that reflect their values, which may diverge. This can lead 
to “splinternets” or digital divergence.
As AI becomes more embedded in public services, healthcare, justice, 
etc., there is stronger demand from citizens and civil society that AI 
be trustworthy, explainable, and non-biased, and for clarity over who 
owns intellectual property, who steers decisions, etc.
Embedding AI models and inference capabilities within edge devices 
(or locally, on-premises) rather than relying almost solely upon 
centralized clouds helps reduce dependency, latency, and exposure 
of sensitive data.
Self-sovereign identity systems and decentralized agents (sometimes 
using blockchain or trusted hardware) are becoming more common, 
giving more control over data and identity to individuals or smaller 
entities.
Building up large AI infrastructure (data centers, high performance 
compute) demands a lot of electricity, cooling, etc. Sovereign 
infrastructure must take into account energy availability, carbon 
footprint, and resilience — otherwise, environmental constraints 
can become the weak link and make digital sovereignty difficult to 
achieve.

To open the door to transitioning from dependence 
to autonomy, your organization should:
□
Engage stakeholders and build resilience: Elevate digital sovereignty 
to the business imperative that it is (i.e., not merely an IT or tech issue); 
involve CISOs, CIOs, legal, compliance, and IT teams; foster a culture of 
data stewardship and sovereignty awareness.
□
Define sovereignty requirements: Specify legal, regulatory, and business 
mandates for data location, access, and control; align with compliance 
obligations (e.g., GDPR, DORA, NIS2, SEC, etc.).
□
Monitor regulatory and geopolitical changes: Track evolving laws and 
frameworks impacting data sovereignty; adapt strategy to new risks.
□
Leverage trusted partners and solutions: Choose vendors that guarantee 
control, transparency, and compliance; partner with providers 
supporting digital sovereignty initiatives.
□
Ensure exit strategies for cloud providers: Include contractual data 
access, usable formats, and retrieval SLAs.

Practical steps to secure digital sovereignty, reduce lock-in, 
and strengthen data resilience
