2
To achieve data sovereignty and support strong 
governance, it’s important to:
	
□
Establish clear data governance policies for acquisition, access, 
stewardship, and lifecycle management.
	
□
Regularly audit and report on data governance to track internal progress 
and to meet evolving regulatory requirements.
	
□
Identify and classify data based on business impact, regulatory 
requirements, and risk exposure; prioritize business-critical data for 
protection and compliance; be sure to engage stakeholders (CISOs, 
CIOs, IT, compliance) in defining and reviewing critical data sets.
	
□
Map dependencies and data flows to understand where critical data 
resides and how it is accessed; leverage transparency features and audit 
logs to track data access and dependencies including cloud providers, 
on-premises systems, and third-party vendors.
	
□
Assess risks related to data residency, sovereignty, and vendor lock-in; 
monitor regulatory changes and geopolitical factors that may impact 
data access or control.
	
□
Develop migration and contingency plans: Decide whether to migrate 
data to a new cloud, to move from cloud to on-prem, or to retain data 
until a new location is available; prepare for operational continuity and 
rapid recovery.
	
□
Implement technical and procedural controls: Enforce physical and 
logical separation of data; use robust encryption and key management 
outside foreign jurisdictions; maintain transparent audit trails and 
compliance monitoring.
When it comes to data backup and recovery in the 
context of digital sovereignty, your organization 
should:
	
□
Engage in scenario planning for migration and recovery: Map out 
scenarios for migrating data between clouds, from cloud to on-
premises, or retaining data until a new location is available; prepare 
contingency plans for rapid recovery and operational continuity.
	
□
Assess vendor independence and platform separation: Ensure backup 
and recovery solutions are vendor-independent and segregated from 
production environments and hyperscaler cloud providers.
	
□
Test recovery plans regularly: Conduct scheduled exercises to validate 
the effectiveness of disaster recovery plans, ensuring teams can restore 
operations quickly and reliably in the event of data loss or disruption.
	
□
Test and validate backup integrity: Regularly test and verify backups; use 
immutable backups and granular restore capabilities.

How Keepit supports digital sovereignty
Given that data sovereignty is a key element of digital sovereignty, it’s critical that your  
organization finds a data protection partner that provides:
•	
Control and ownership: Ensure the provider has complete control over its data and management planes. This 
eliminates third-party risks (such as sub-processors) and ensures that you remain compliant with local and 
international data regulations.
•	
Physical and logical separation: Look for vendors that guarantee physical and logical separation  
from production environments.
•	
Transparency and auditability: Verify that the solution provides transparent audit trails and  
compliance monitoring.
•	
Cost and performance control: Choose a vendor that allows you to predict and manage costs effectively while 
maintaining optimal performance.
•	
Regulatory alignment: Ensure the provider is aligned with local laws and global standards to avoid  
legal complications.
For Keepit, digital sovereignty isn’t a theoretical ideal — it’s a cornerstone of modern cybersecurity.
Where traditional SaaS data protection vendors rely heavily on third-party infrastructure, Keepit takes a 
radically different approach, maintaining full control over both the data and management planes, both 
of which are physically and logically separated from production environments. This independence from 
hyperscalers protects our users from hidden dependencies and indirect access paths.
Our unique architecture means that Keepit controls cost, functionality, security, performance, 
management, operations, and integration — ensuring that customers are not at the mercy of hyperscalers 
or foreign policies.
In an era where sovereignty risks are growing, Keepit stands as a beacon of control and reliability. By 
partnering with us, your organization can confidently navigate the complexities of today’s evolving 
cybersecurity challenges and regulatory requirements with a modern solution that ensuring data is secure, 
compliant, and ready to support innovative business initiatives.
To learn more about how Keepit can support your data protection and cybersecurity needs,  
please visit us at keepit.com.
Conclusion
Key takeaways:
•	 Digital sovereignty is not a one-time goal, but an ongoing process. Now is the 
right time for leaders of organizations around the world to accept responsibility 
and to take the necessary steps to secure their digital independence.
•	 Only through conscious decisions and the choice of sovereign solutions can organizations 
secure and maintain control over their digital futures and sovereignty over their data.

Introduction
Your development stack is more than tools. It’s your product roadmap, your intellectual property, your 
velocity, and your institutional knowledge. Platforms like Jira, Confluence, and GitHub sit at the center 
of how modern teams build and ship software. 
 
But two recent realities are forcing a rethink: 
•	
The shift away from on-premises support by Atlassian is accelerating cloud dependence 
•	
Even leading platforms can experience data integrity issues, including incidents impacting pull/
merge requests 
And here’s the uncomfortable truth: If your collaboration and development data is lost, corrupted, or 
overwritten, most native protections won’t bring it back the way you need. 
 
Here’s a quick checklist to help you quickly assess your exposure: 
1. Do you have source code and repository protection?
Organizations that have built strong safeguards around their development data can 
recover deleted repositories, branches, and commits to a precise point in time, supported 
by independent backups. They can also restore pull requests, merge history, and commit 
metadata, preserving the full context of development activity. Protections against accidental 
or automated deletions further reduce risk, ensuring code integrity and continuity across the 
software lifecycle. 
 
Without these capabilities, development environments become highly vulnerable. Lost re-
positories or corrupted history are difficult—if not impossible—to fully reconstruct, especially 
without external backups or metadata. Even small deletions can cascade into broken builds 
and stalled workflows. Left unchecked, this risk leads to permanent loss of code history, 
unrecoverable development work, and significant disruption to engineering productivity.
2. Do you have work management and ticketing resilience?
Organizations that have strong control over their work management data and processes 
can recover issues, tickets, and workflows, along with historical sprint data and backlog 
prioritization. Automation rules and custom workflows can be restored, and version history 
provides visibility into changes over time. This ensures continuity across planning, execution, 
and delivery, even in the face of disruption. 
 
Without these capabilities, operational visibility and coordination quickly break down. Lost 
tickets, missing sprint data, or broken workflows disrupt planning and execution, while the 
lack of version history makes it difficult to understand or fix issues. Left unchecked, this 
results in loss of product planning, delivery tracking, and overall operational continuity.

3
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
3. Do you have knowledge and documentation continuity?
Organizations that have strong safeguards in place for preserving institutional knowledge 
can restore pages, spaces, and attachments, with historical versions fully recoverable to 
maintain accuracy and context. Critical runbooks and internal documentation are backed up 
independently, and permissions and access structures can be restored, ensuring the right 
people retain access to the right information. This supports smooth onboarding, consistent 
operations, and continuity of knowledge across teams. 
 
Without these capabilities, knowledge loss becomes a real risk. Missing documentation, lost 
version history, or broken permissions create confusion and slow teams down. Onboarding 
becomes more difficult without reliable resources, and day-to-day operations are impacted 
by gaps in information. Left unchecked, this results in loss of institutional knowledge, 
increased friction, and operational delays.
4. Do you have ransomware and insider threat protection?
Organizations that have built strong protections for collaboration and development data 
integrity ensure code, tickets, and documentation are stored immutably, so they cannot 
be altered or deleted, and backups are isolated from production environments to prevent 
attackers from compromising both at once. Teams can roll back malicious or unauthorized 
changes and rely on tested recovery scenarios for compromised developer accounts. This 
enables a clean, controlled recovery that preserves trust in development systems. 
 
Without these protections, the risk is severe. Attackers or unauthorized changes can corrupt 
code, tickets, and documentation—and potentially impact backups—eliminating any reliable 
recovery point. Without the ability to roll back changes or execute a proven recovery process, 
issues can spread quickly across systems. Left unchecked, this results in widespread data 
corruption with no clean path to recovery, forcing prolonged disruption and complex rebuild 
efforts. 
5. Do you have operational recovery capabilities?
Organizations that have built a recovery model that supports both speed and precision 
across their collaboration and development environment can perform full environment 
restores across tools while also executing fast, granular recovery of repositories, tickets, or 
documentation. Recovery time objectives (RTOs) are clearly defined and achievable, and 
the process does not rely on manual exports or scripts. This ensures consistent, predictable 
recovery and keeps engineering teams productive even during disruptions. 
 
Without these capabilities, recovery becomes slow and error-prone. Limited restore options, 
unclear RTOs, and reliance on manual processes introduce delays and inconsistencies. Even 
small issues can escalate into broader outages that stall development work. Left unchecked, 
this results in prolonged downtime and significant loss of engineering productivity.

4
6. Do you have platform dependency and change risk?
Organizations that have reduced their dependence on vendors for data protection and 
recovery don’t rely solely on native retention policies and are prepared for platform-level 
changes, such as shifts to cloud-only models. With the ability to recover data independently 
of vendor availability and clear contingency plans for service disruptions, they maintain 
control and continuity regardless of external changes. 
 
Without these capabilities, organizations are tightly coupled to vendor performance and 
decisions. Changes to platforms, outages, or limited retention policies can quickly disrupt 
access to critical data. If recovery depends on the vendor, options become limited during 
incidents. Left unchecked, this risk results in vendor-driven disruptions that directly impact 
your ability to operate.
7. Do you have compliance, audit and IP protection?
Organizations that have strong governance and protection in place for their development and 
operational data maintain audit trails of changes across repositories and tickets, can support 
legal hold and forensic investigations, and ensure backup data aligns with compliance 
requirements. Intellectual property is further protected through independent recovery, giving 
teams the ability to restore critical assets without relying on a single system. This creates 
defensibility, traceability, and confidence in how data is managed and protected. 
 
Without these capabilities, organizations face significant legal and compliance exposure. 
Limited auditability, inability to support investigations, and gaps in backup coverage 
make it difficult to prove control over data. Intellectual property becomes vulnerable to 
loss or compromise without a reliable recovery path. Left unchecked, this risk can lead to 
compliance failures, legal challenges, and increased exposure of critical assets.
Now, assess your risk
If you can’t say “yes” to all these questions, then it’s time to take a deep-dive into better 
understanding your vulnerabilities. Request a meeting with a Keepit resilience expert to assess 
potential gaps in the protection and recoverability of your critical data across Jira, Confluence, and 
GitHub. 
Better understand your organization’s exposure to data loss, operational disruption, and platform-
related risk before missing code, tickets, or documentation impact delivery and business continuity.

This report examines the reality of SaaS data loss caused by four common 
scenarios through relevant, real-world examples alongside realistic (yet hypo-
thetical) situations and asks a practical question: When there’s a disruption to 
production, who’s in control of the data and how is business continuity ensured? 
The four Ms of data loss show how control is lost, while immutable, independent 
backup plus practiced recovery, sound data governance, and considered data 
sovereignty show how control is maintained or regained.
One thing is clear: Cyber resilience in the SaaS era is not a one-time restore 
exercise. Instead it needs to be a broader strategy shaped by how data is lost, 
how recovery is tested, how backup data is stored, how readiness matures, and 
whether control remains under the sovereignty and dependency conditions an 
organization faces, both from inside and external compliance demands.
Paul Robichaux
Microsoft MVP, Senior Director 
of Product at Keepit

Executive summary
SaaS changes disaster recovery because application 
availability and data recoverability are no longer owned by 
the same entity.
Most SaaS data loss comes from four recurring sources: 
malicious attacks, mistakes by admins, mishaps at the 
cloud provider, and migrations gone bad.
Resilience depends on independent backup, tested 
recovery, identity-aware restoration, and a realistic 
maturity path — not on optimistic assumptions about 
native protections.
Sovereignty matters because data is not truly resilient  
if it’s not stored within an infrastructure you control or  
have complete transparency into.

The SaaS data protection gap
Responsibility in the disaster recovery equation
Cloud adoption made a lot of things easier, but it also introduced the shared responsibility model that every 
SaaS provider champions. One of the biggest changes is that application availability as well as data avail-
ability and recoverability are no longer owned by the same entity, leading to a data protection gap stemming 
from a common misunderstanding of what is protected and by whom.
Along with these changes to application and data responsibilities, cybercriminals are targeting these cloud 
services aggressively. Compliance requirements keep rising, including the need for measured data sover-
eignty, which has moved from a legal edge case to a board-level resilience question. On top of all of this, AI 
is speeding up both administration and data creation, as well as increasing the magnitude of mistakes and 
lowering the bar of entry for cybercriminals.
Most organizations already have some form of business continuity or disaster recovery plan, but the data 
protection gap remains as many of those plans treat SaaS data as if it’s automatically protected (it’s not) 
by the application provider through native backup offerings. The shared responsibility model applies, 
which tells us: The SaaS provider runs the service, but the customer remains responsible for data, identities, 
configurations, access, and recoverability (as well as for the risks and compliance requirements placed on 
that data).
Figure 1. The shared responsibility model highlights the user’s responsibilities for data, identity, and more.
A recent CIO MarketPulse white paper highlights this gap: More than one third of surveyed organizations still 
rely entirely on native SaaS protections. Nearly half have already suffered a major data loss event, and 37% 
still do nothing beyond native protection. Confidence also runs ahead of readiness: 53% of respondents 
believe they could recover from a major data loss within 24 hours, yet 11% say it would take a month or more 
— or that they may not be able to fully recover at all.
Confidence in recovery speed after data loss

Within a month

than a month

might not be possible
 
Figure 2. Survey data reflects on SaaS data loss recovery readiness confidence. Source: CIO MarketPulse white paper.

What makes this especially important is that SaaS data loss rarely arrives as one cinematic catastro-
phe. It’s just as likely to come from everyday failures: an admin mistake, a retention-policy change, a 
provider-side incident, or a migration that quietly goes wrong. That is why disaster recovery for SaaS 
data is not simply an “any backup will do” conversation, but a cyber resilience conversation bolstered 
by independent, sovereign backup and tested and proven recovery.
 
SaaS data loss survey
Figure 3. Survey data shows SaaS data loss comes from multiple causes, not just cyberattacks. Source:  ESG report
This is also why cyber resilience in SaaS is broader than backup alone. It includes controlled access to clean 
data while the production environment is unstable, safe restoration once that environment is healthy again, 
and governance decisions about where the recovery path lives and who ultimately controls it, all of which 
demand backup data being stored outside of the domain of the SaaS provider/hyperscale cloud.

Disaster recovery guide   |   6
The SaaS data protection gap

Keeping control
What cyber resilience looks like in a SaaS disruption
In an on-premises model, meeting a recovery time objective is largely about recovering systems and the data 
they store. The organization owns both layers, so the recovery model is more unified. In SaaS, the provider 
operates the application, but the customer still carries the consequences of lost, corrupted, inaccessible, 
or legally constrained data. That means resilience has to be understood in terms of control: control over 
accessible backup copies, control over identity and access management, control over data sovereignty and 
governance, and control over the environment and obligations that shape recovery.
Access during disruption
How completely and quickly can critical 
data be accessed, even if the SaaS appli-
cation, tenant, or control place is unhealthy 
or down?
Restore after recovery
How completely and quickly can that data 
be restored once the application tenant 
is operational again — and in the order the 
business actually needs?
That split is easy to overlook because SaaS vendors understandably talk about uptime and service resil-
ience. But availability of the service is not the same as recoverability of the customer’s data. Shared respon-
sibility does not end at service availability, but rather it defines who owns the risk. The provider is responsible 
for running the platform; the customer is still responsible for ensuring that business-critical data, identity 
structures, and recovery paths remain protected, independent, and usable when things go wrong.
The key takeaway
You can outsource operations, but you can’t outsource accountability.
Ransomware is the clearest example of why this matters. Modern attacks are designed to do more than 
encrypt files. They try to break trust in production data, disable recovery options, and force a business into a 
time-compressed decision. Ransomware-as-a-service lowered the barrier to entry. Attackers increasingly 
target backups because weakening the recovery path is often faster than negotiating. That’s why resilience 
depends on more than “having copies.” Those copies need meaningful separation, logical air-gapping, 
immutability, and a recovery path the attacker cannot easily touch.
Data governance and data sovereignty add the next layer. Governance defines what must be protected, 
retained, restored, and reviewed, while sovereignty defines which laws, regulations, compliance obliga-
tions, providers, and jurisdictions shape that protection. Together with shared responsibility, they go a long 
way toward determining whether an organization truly controls its SaaS data or not. In practice, that control 
is achieved through immutable, independent, air-gapped backup and tested recovery. This is the context in 
which the four Ms framing becomes useful.
Disaster recovery guide   |   7
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved

The four Ms of data loss 
Malice, mistakes, mishaps, and migrations
A practical way to frame the incidents most organizations actually face 
Figure 4. A practical way to frame the incidents most organizations actually face.
Malicious attacks
Ransomware, credential abuse, destructive compromise, and attempts to delete or 
corrupt the recovery path itself.
Mistakes by admins
Retention missteps, accidental deletions, misconfigurations, overprivileged automation, 
and rushed changes in production.
Mishaps at your cloud provider
Outages, control-plane defects, synchronization errors, and provider-side failures that 
remove access or trust in production. 
Migrations gone bad
Tenant moves, M&A projects, divestitures, cutovers, sync failures, and bulk changes 
that are hard to unwind after the fact.
Data loss rarely happens as a single, random event. In practice, most incidents follow recognizable patterns 
that make them easier to plan for than they first appear. One useful way to frame those patterns is through 
the four Ms of data loss: malicious attacks, mistakes by admins, mishaps at the cloud provider, and migra-
tions gone bad. Each category shows a different way control can be lost, whether through attack, error, 
dependency, or change.
This framework matters because it moves the conversation from abstract risk to operational control. The 
causes differ, but the business question is usually the same: Can the organization identify a trusted recovery 
point, restore the right data quickly enough to limit disruption, and do so under conditions it can trust and 
control? Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report reinforces why that framing holds up. Third-party 
involvement in breaches doubled to 30%, exploitation of vulnerabilities rose 34%, and credential abuse 
remained one of the most common initial access patterns. Some disruptions are malicious, some are struc-
tural, and many begin somewhere in between.
Not every incident is a cyberattack. Some begin with a bad retention change, an integration failure, or a 
provider-side event that makes the control plane unreliable. The common thread is that production can stop 
being the sole source of truth. Resilience then depends on regaining control through independent backup, 
practiced recovery, good governance, and sovereignty-minded design.

of the 4 Ms  here →

Malicious attacks
Malicious attacks are among the most disruptive causes of data loss because they are designed to compro-
mise both the production environment and the organization’s ability to recover from it. Ransomware, 
credential abuse, destructive compromise, and malicious deletion all aim at the same outcome: break trust 
in production, degrade access, and turn time into leverage. In SaaS environments, that often means the 
recovery sequence matters just as much as the backup itself. You may need to restore identities before data, 
re-establish permissions before access, and verify that the tenant is safe before pushing content back into it.
A published INNOVISION case shows why that sequencing matters. The customer had recently deployed 
independent backup for Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 after recognizing that cloud workloads still 
needed their own protection. Soon after, the environment was hit by a targeted cyberattack. Because the 
recovery path was already in place, the organization was able to restore all impacted Entra ID user accounts 
and associated Microsoft 365 data with a recovery time of less than three hours. Restoring the compromised 
identities first avoided a slower, manual rebuild in which user accounts would have needed to be recreated 
one by one, complete with undocumented settings, permissions, and dependencies. That’s an important 
SaaS lesson: In a cloud incident, restoring content without restoring the identity layer can still leave the busi-
ness operationally stuck.
PROBLEM
RECOVERY
The company was hit by a targeted cyberattack, 
compromising user identities on Entra ID.
They were able to quickly restore all impacted Entra 
ID user accounts, along with their Microsoft 365 data 
with an RTO of less than three hours.
REAL CASE
A CUSTOMER OF OUR PARTNER INNOVISION
READ THE CASE HERE →
The same INNOVISION recovery story also shows that backup can matter after the restore, not just during 
it. While it is the speed of recovery that’s essential during, it is completeness of recovery after that matters. 
During the post-incident investigation and cyber-insurance process, the customer needed evidence of 
what had changed in Entra ID objects and when. Metadata differencing was used to trace attribute-level 
changes on privileged objects and provide technical evidence for the postmortem. That expands the role 
of backup from restoration into investigation, documentation, and incident validation, and makes it a critical 
part for being able to secure cyber insurance.
The Technology Did It case makes a different point: the integrity of the backup path itself. In that case, a U.S. 
government supplier was hit by Conti ransomware roughly three months after onboarding. According to the 
published account, the protected data remained unavailable to the attacker, the organization restored its 
data back to SharePoint, all data was restored within 30 minutes, and the business was back to normal by 
Monday morning after a Friday attack. The headline is speed, but the deeper point is separation. Recovery 
was fast because the recovery copies were still trustworthy, immutable to the impacts of ransomware.

encrypting their business-critical data.
The protected backup data remained immutable and the 
company was able to restore all data in time to continue 
business operations as usual on monday morning

The four Ms of data loss: Malicious attacks

A third example from an SMB customer organization in education is useful for a quieter reason. The attack 
affected the organization’s Microsoft 365 environment while backups were still running, but the business 
still had access to a last-known-good snapshot from before the corruption spread. That gave the team a 
clean point in time to recover from rather than forcing it to trust the production environment after the fact. 
In ransomware and destructive-attack scenarios, that distinction is everything. The question is not whether 
data still exists somewhere — it’s whether a clean, usable recovery point exists outside the compromised 
environment.

The value of backup is not merely that a copy exists, it’s that the organization can identify a clean point in time, 
restore both business data and identity components in the right order, and support investigation once the 
immediate disruption is contained. 
How control is regained: Keep clean, immutable backup copies outside the production trust boundary, 
practice restoring identities as well as content, and use backup metadata to support investigation, not 
just restoration.
How control is regained
•	Keep clean immutable backup copies outside the production trust boundary
•	Practice restoring identities as well as content
•	Use backup metadata to support investigation, not just restoration.
Recovery tip
Plan for malicious incidents on the assumption that both production data and the recovery path 
will be targeted. Resilience here depends on immutable, logically isolated, operationally inde-
pendent backups — and on knowing the order in which critical identity and business data need to 
come back. See also: Why backups are targeted.

Disaster recovery guide   |   10
The four Ms of data loss: Malicious attacks

Mistakes by admins
Administrative mistakes are a common source of SaaS data loss because they happen with legitimate 
access, often in live production, and frequently before anyone recognizes the downstream impact. In SaaS 
environments, the blast radius can extend well beyond the obvious deleted object. A rushed retention 
change can alter legal-hold behavior. A policy edit can’t be undone. A deleted identity object can break 
application access, automation, and approvals in one move.
One customer example involving a large retail chain specializing in home furnishing, makes the point clearly. 
A retention setting in the tenant was accidentally changed from five years to one year, and the result was 
not a minor correction but the need to restore several thousand mailboxes. The lesson is not only that policy 
mistakes are easy to make, but that recovering from them often requires more than bringing back message 
content. Mailbox structure, metadata, state, and context still have to be usable after the restore. In poli-
cy-driven environments like Microsoft 365, a single admin action can therefore become a large operational 
recovery event.
PROBLEM
RECOVERY
An accidental change in a retention setting resulted in the 
loss of several thousand Microsoft Exchange mailboxes.
The company was able to restore the mailboxes with 
mailbox structure, metadata, state, and context intact. 
REAL CASE
PRIVATE ENTERPRISE IN RETAIL  —  EMEA
Identity mistakes can be even more punishing. Consider accidental deletion of a security group, app registra-
tion, or enterprise application. If the deleted object controls access to critical business tools, employees can 
lose access immediately, integrations can fail, and permissions may have to be rebuilt manually. Microsoft’s 
own recovery guidance on restoring app registrations and restoring soft-deleted enterprise applications 
makes clear that native recovery exists only for a limited period. After 30 days, those objects are permanent-
ly deleted. Even inside the recovery window, restoring the object alone is not always enough. Relationships 
— memberships, owners, assignments, connected links — are often what make the object usable in the first 
place. That’s why identity-aware recovery, including cross-tenant restore, matters in practice.
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
Disaster recovery guide   |   11
The four Ms of data loss: Mistakes by admins

AI adds a new twist to this category, but not a new principle. In a recent TechCrunch example, a Meta AI 
security researcher asked an OpenClaw agent to review an overstuffed inbox and suggest what to delete 
or archive. Instead, the agent began deleting emails outright and ignored attempts to stop it from a phone, 
forcing direct intervention on the device running the tool. Publicly, that reads as an AI-agent mishap. Opera-
tionally, it’s an administrative error amplified by automation: destructive authority was granted, live data was 
used, and the controls around scale and approval were weaker than the task required. The mistake was not 
just the click, but the trust model around the automation.
That’s the broader lesson for this category. “Mistakes by admins” doesn’t just mean someone pressed the 
wrong button, it includes excessive permissions, rushed production changes, poorly scoped automa-
tion, and the move from test data to live data without adequate safeguards. In these scenarios, recovery 
depends on having versioned, external backups that preserve not only content but also metadata, object 
relationships, and identity structures.
How control is regained
•	Narrow destructive authority
•	Protect policy states and identity objects
•	Make sure backup preserves relationships and history — not just content.
Recovery tip
Your backup strategy has to account for people — the tired ones, the rushed ones, the overcon-
fident ones, and the well-meaning ones who just made a bad change. Use external, versioned 
backups that can restore clean data, metadata, and relationships even when the disruption came 
from legitimate access.
“No matter how well-trained your admins are, they’re always 
under crushing pressure to do more, faster, with less. Mistakes 
are guaranteed to happen. The problem is, with today’s systems, 
and especially with AI, a small mistake can have a giant impact.“
Paul Robichaux, Senior Director of Product at Keepit and Microsoft MVP
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
Disaster recovery guide   |   12
The four Ms of data loss: Mistakes by admins

Mishaps at your cloud provider
Cloud providers are highly resilient, but not infallible. Service failures, configuration defects, synchronization 
issues, control-plane bugs, and cascading dependencies can affect availability, access, or trust in produc-
tion data even when the customer did nothing wrong. These events belong in their own category because 
the root cause sits with the provider, but the operational consequences still land squarely on the customer.
Microsoft’s Azure Front Door post-incident review from late October 2025 is a useful example. According 
to Microsoft, a specific sequence of valid customer configuration changes across different control-plane 
build versions generated incompatible metadata that exposed a latent bug in the Azure Front Door data 
plane. The resulting failure caused connection timeouts and DNS resolution issues across Azure Front Door 
and Azure CDN, with knock-on impact to Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, Entra ID services, 
and even support-case creation. This detail matters because it shows how mature cloud environments can 
still fail in non-obvious ways: not through one dramatic hardware outage, but through interaction between 
control-plane versions, metadata, and protection logic.
The incident is also a reminder that resiliency safeguards have limits. Microsoft noted that configuration 
protections and “last known good” controls did not stop the problem because the metadata passed available 
checks before the asynchronous failure surfaced. Recovery required manual intervention, blocking further 
configuration propagation, editing the last-known-good configuration, and phased recovery across the 
fleet. For customers, the takeaway is not that hyperscalers are unreliable, but rather that customer continuity 
cannot depend entirely on the assumption that provider-side safeguards will always behave as designed.
This is where shared responsibility stops being a slogan and becomes an operating model. The provider is 
responsible for the infrastructure and service availability it delivers, while the customer is still responsible 
for data, identities, configurations, retention decisions, backup practices, and recovery readiness. Not 
every provider incident is a direct data-loss event: some are availability or access-path incidents. But from 
the customer’s perspective, the question is the same: Can critical data still be reached and recovered if the 
production platform is unstable or unavailable?
How control is regained
Treat provider-side incidents as continuity events, not somebody else’s problem. If the control plane 
is unstable, you still need an independent path to clean data and a plan for what business can oper-
ate from backup.
Recovery tip
Treat provider-side incidents as proof that availability and recoverability are different problems. 
Your vendor restores the service, but you still need an independent recovery path for the business 
data, identities, and configurations that keep operations moving.
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
Disaster recovery guide   |   13
The four Ms of data loss

Migration gone bad
Migration-related loss is usually not dramatic until it’s expensive. It happens when users, mailboxes, files, 
permissions, collaboration spaces, or identity objects move from one environment to another and the 
move introduces omissions, duplication, corruption, or data mixing that is difficult to unwind after the fact. 
In Microsoft 365 especially, tenant-to-tenant moves tied to mergers, acquisitions, divestitures, and reorga-
nization are common enough that Microsoft treats them as standard migration scenarios, not edge cases.
A realistic example is pharmaceutical divestiture. A business unit is sold, and a defined set of employees, 
mailboxes, OneDrive data, SharePoint sites, groups, and permissions must move into a new tenant. Before 
the migration even starts, both sides have reasons to verify exactly what belongs where. If the migration fails 
halfway through, if content is omitted, or if data from the retained business is mixed into the divested envi-
ronment, the organization needs a known-good record of the source state. Without that reference point, 
it becomes much harder to prove what should have moved, what should have stayed behind, and whether 
sensitive or commercially important information ended up in the wrong place.
PROBLEM
RECOVERY
A problem occurs during migration and content is omitted, 
or data from the retained business is mixed into the divested 
environment.
With a known-good record of the source state, the 
organization can restore data to the trusted pre-migration 
baseline before starting the process over. 
HYPOTHETICAL CASE
PHARMACEUTICAL ENTERPRISE
That’s why backup matters in a migration even when no attack has taken place. It creates a trusted pre-mi-
gration baseline that can be used to validate the move, investigate discrepancies, and restore clean source 
data if the project introduces errors. In carve-outs and divestitures, that baseline is not just technically 
useful, it can become legally important. Missing, misplaced, or over-shared data can quickly turn into 
disputes about what was actually transferred.
How control is regained
•	Take a validated point-in-time backup before cutover
•	Keep a trustworthy source baseline until the migration is complete and verified.
Recovery tip
Treat migrations like disaster scenarios. Take complete, point-in-time backups before cutover, 
decide what must be provable afterward, and test recovery as part of the migration plan. Other-
wise, you may discover that yesterday’s lunch menu is easy to restore while the data the business 
actually needs is still tied up in the project.
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
Disaster recovery guide   |   14
The four Ms of data loss

Resilience is backup + tested recovery
Backup isn’t a checkbox. Disaster recovery resilience is immutable, independent backup plus tested, veri-
fied recovery. A backup that exists in theory but has never been exercised under realistic conditions is still 
only part of the job. Backup and recovery become resilience when the organization has tested the incidents 
it’s actually likely to face, measured the results, and improved the process. Backup is necessary, but it 
becomes operationally meaningful only when the business has proved it can recover with it.
Practiced recovery is rarely a single technical action. More often, it’s a sequence of dependencies, deci-
sions, and timing constraints. An organization needs to know what must come back first, which business 
processes depend on that order, how identity and content interact, and whether acceptable recovery 
objectives can actually be met in practice rather than assumed in theory. Testing is what exposes weak 
sequencing, fuzzy ownership, and hidden dependencies before an incident does.
The right tests are scenario-based. That means exercising recovery from the incidents the organization is 
actually likely to face: ransomware, large-scale admin error, provider-side disruption, identity corruption, 
and bulk restore — not just single-item recovery. A test that proves someone can restore one deleted file 
may still say almost nothing about whether the business can recover a tenant-wide failure or a compromised 
identity layer. Importantly, bulk restore isn’t theoretical: Keepit’s Annual Data Report shows 9 in 10 enterprise 
and commercial-size organizations validate bulk recovery at least once a year —suggesting that at scale, 
bulk restore testing is already a standard marker of recovery maturity.”
 
KEEPIT ANNUAL DATA REPORT 2026:
See what the data reveals here →
Identity deserves its own testing track. In Microsoft 365 environments, Entra ID is the control layer for access, 
roles, policies, groups, app registrations, and service principals. Testing should therefore not stop at files, 
mailboxes, or collaboration data. Organizations also need to validate whether identity objects and their 
relationships can be rebuilt in a separate clean tenant if the primary tenant is compromised, unavailable, or 
simply no longer trustworthy. That’s why cross-tenant restore is more of a control question than a product 
feature discussion. 
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
Disaster recovery guide   |   15
 Resilience is backup + tested recovery

Keepit’s Annual Data Report flags identity recovery as a persistent blind spot: Organizations test identity 
restores roughly four times less often than productivity data restores. That gap matters because if Entra ID 
can’t be recovered cleanly, access to Microsoft 365, and often every other SaaS system federated to it, may 
be blocked even when the underlying data is intact. 
It’s also worth noting that this comparison is drawn from organizations that already have an Entra ID back-
up/recovery capability in place—so it reflects a gap that can persist even among teams that are relatively 
advanced in their recovery posture.
Testing is also getting harder to separate from governance. Whether the driver is DORA, SEC expectations, 
FINRA expectations, or internal audit pressure, the direction is the same: Organizations increasingly need 
to show not only that data is protected, but that it can be restored in a controlled, reliable way when need-
ed. Navigating SEC and FINRA regulations makes the same point from a different angle: Recovery testing 
provides operational proof. It shows that backup is not just a policy artifact or a retention mechanism, but a 
workable part of the resilience strategy — and that the organization can recover on terms it understands and 
controls.
Recovery tip
Treat testing as a standing resilience practice rather than a one-time validation exercise. 
The goal is to confirm that backup data is independent, intact, and usable in realistic scenarios — and 
that the organization can restore the right data and identity elements in the right sequence when an 
incident occurs.

 Resilience is backup + tested recovery

From testing cadence to recovery maturity
Survey data suggests that disaster recovery testing is becoming more established, and that is encouraging. 
In the latest CIO MarketPulse report, 54% of respondents said they test quarterly and 32% said they test 
monthly. But cadence alone does not define readiness. 
Frequency of disaster recovery plan testing
Figure 5. Recovery testing is becoming more routine, but cadence alone does not guarantee readiness. Source: CIO MarketPulse report
A monthly test of a narrow scenario is still narrow. An organization can test often and still have weak docu-
mentation, unclear ownership, or blind spots around identity and control-plane recovery. And this problem 
is intensified by the wide-spread adoption of AI: As agentic AI adoption spreads from centralized IT teams 
into the wider organization, even small blind spots can disrupt incident response and recovery. There is often 
a gap between perceived readiness and real-world recovery capability, and what surprises teams is how 
many steps sit between having a backup and actually being operational again when an incident occurs.

From testing cadence to recovery maturity

SaaS disaster recovery maturity
That’s why maturity matters. For many organizations, the problem is not understanding that disaster recovery 
is important, it’s knowing where the current capability really stands, where the biggest gaps are, and what 
the next most valuable improvement should be. A SaaS-specific maturity framework is useful because resil-
ience isn’t so black and white as a yes or no: An organization can have backups and still lack clear ownership, 
scenario coverage, documentation, or sovereignty-aware recovery design.
Figure 6. A practical maturity path moves teams from reactive recovery toward managed resilience.  
Related framework: SaaS disaster recovery maturity framework.
Keepit’s SaaS disaster recovery maturity framework uses five stages — reactive, basic, structured, proac-
tive, and managed — to make that progression tangible. Reactive teams recover ad hoc, depend on individ-
ual heroics, and often discover the process while the incident is happening. Basic teams have some back-
ups and some repeatable steps, but coverage and testing are inconsistent. Structured teams document 
procedures, assign owners, and bring regular testing into the process. Proactive teams measure, improve, 
and exercise scenarios before crisis reveals the gaps. Managed teams integrate recovery with governance, 
compliance, communications, and broader business continuity.
MATURITY FRAMEWORK:
Find out how mature your  
DR processes are here →
According to the CIO MarketPulse report “Peer insights on AI adoption and the disaster recovery gap,” when 
respondents rated the maturity of their current SaaS disaster recovery capabilities, 14% placed themselves 
in a reactive state, 26% in a developing stage, 32% in a managed stage, and 28% in an optimized stage. In 
other words, while regular testing appears relatively common, not every organization has translated that 
activity into a fully integrated, continuously improving disaster recovery capability.

broader business operations as a core function.

Disaster recovery guide   |   18
From testing cadence to recovery maturity

One of the strengths of a maturity model is that it discourages perfection theater. Most organizations 
do not become ‘managed’ by buying one more tool. They advance by moving to the next stage on 
purpose: documenting recovery procedures, clarifying responsibilities, identifying business-critical 
SaaS data and identity dependencies, introducing more regular and realistic testing, and then building 
measurement and continuous improvement on top of that foundation.
Maturity is also rarely uniform. An organization can be strong on executive motivation or compliance pressure 
and still be weak on documentation, staffing, or scenario coverage. The point of the model is not to award a 
flattering label. It is to help the organization orient itself honestly and choose the next improvement that will 
make the biggest operational difference.

From testing cadence to recovery maturity
”Ultimately, maturity in disaster recovery isn’t about achieving perfection, 
it’s about pursuing it. Building a sustainable capability to protect what 
matters most, and recover it quickly when you need to — that’s the imperative 
we all share. You have to be able to do that no matter what challenges 
arise. Even small improvements in your DR planning compound to help 
dramatically reduce your overall risk. And that reduction in risk quickly builds 
confidence in your organization’s ability to withstand disruptions.”
Paul Robichaux, Senior Director of Product at Keepit and Microsoft MVP

Governance and sovereignty 
define the terms of control
Data sovereignty has moved from a niche legal concern to a broader resilience and governance issue. It’s 
no longer just a question of where data sits on a map, but rather a question of which laws apply to it, who 
can compel access to it, which providers and sub-processors sit in the dependency chain, and whether the 
organization retains meaningful control over how data is protected and recovered.
The shared responsibility and sovereignty discussion captures the shift well: Shared responsibility answers 
who owns the risk; sovereignty shapes the conditions under which that risk has to be managed. That distinc-
tion matters because sovereignty is often misunderstood as simple residency. In practice, residency is 
only one layer of the issue. Data may be created in one country, processed in another, stored in a third, and 
backed up in a fourth. And for data governance, organizations need to know what data exists, which retention 
and compliance obligations apply, who can access it, which provider and sub-processor dependencies sit 
behind it, and whether recovery can happen without recreating the same exposure. If the production SaaS 
provider and the backup provider depend on the same underlying hyperscaler or legal jurisdiction, an orga-
nization may have redundancy without true independence. That’s why the broader data sovereignty report 
treats sovereignty as part of resilience planning, not as a separate compliance checkbox.
DATA SOVEREIGNTY REPORT:
Read more about data 
sovereignty here →
A useful way to think about this is that sovereignty introduces a second layer of recovery readiness. The first 
layer asks whether data can be restored, while the second asks whether it is stored (and can be restored) 
under conditions the organization controls and can trust: in the right jurisdiction, with clear access, and with-
out being trapped by the same dependencies that may have contributed to the original disruption. If the 
answer to the first question is yes but the answer to the second is unclear, resilience is still incomplete.
Put differently, shared responsibility says you still own the data risk, and sovereignty says you also own the 
rules and obligations attached to that data. Together, they determine whether you control your SaaS data or 
not in a much broader sense.
Questions worth asking now
	
□
Who controls the infrastructure on which both production and backup depend?
	
□
Which jurisdictions can assert authority over the data or the backup provider?
	
□
Are production and backup tied to the same hyperscaler, region, or legal dependency chain?
	
□
Can the organization prove those answers when an incident, audit, or geopolitical event makes 
them matter?

RECOMMENDATION
What to do next
1
Identify which SaaS data and identity services must be restored 
first for the business to keep operating.
2
Separate backup from production dependencies and validate 
that backup data is genuinely immutable and independently 
accessible.
3
Extend recovery scope beyond files to include metadata, roles, 
policies, app relationships, and identity objects.
4
Run scenario-based tests that include bulk restore and identity 
recovery — not just single-item restore.
5
Use a maturity framework to prioritize the next improvement of 
your disaster recovery planning.
6
Review sovereignty and dependency together: retention, 
jurisdiction, sub-processor exposure, compliance obligations, 
and who can authorize recovery.

Disaster recovery guide   |   21
Governance and sovereignty define the terms of control

Conclusion
The central lesson of SaaS disaster recovery is simple: The cloud changed the location of the 
problem, not the consequences of losing data, as well as introducing the shared responsibility 
models which all SaaS providers employ. Whether the trigger is malicious, mistaken, provid-
er-side, or migration-related, the business still has to answer the same core questions under 
pressure: Can we access clean data, can we restore it in the right order, and can we do so in an 
environment we trust and control?
The four Ms of data loss show how control is lost, while resilience shows how control is regained 
— through immutable, independent backup, practiced recovery, disciplined governance, and 
sovereignty-aware design. The organizations that get there are not necessarily the ones with 
the boldest claims about resilience, they’re the ones that understand data loss happens, test 
realistic scenarios, include identity and bulk restore in those tests, know where they sit on the 
maturity curve, and treat sovereignty and dependency questions as part of the design rather 
than as afterthoughts.
Independent, sovereign backup plus tested, verified recovery is disaster recovery resilience. 
And in SaaS, resilience is ultimately about control: knowing your data is protected, recoverable, 
and governed on terms you know and can trust.

Introduction
Identity is now the operational and security control plane of modern business. Platforms like Microsoft 
Entra ID and Okta don’t just manage access: they control how employees work, how systems 
communicate, and how organizations operate securely at scale. 
As identity environments become more interconnected and automated, attackers are increasingly 
targeting Identity Access Management (IAM) systems through ransomware, compromised privileged 
accounts, configuration manipulation, and AI-enhanced phishing and social engineering attacks. 
Yet many organizations still rely primarily on native protections designed for availability, not 
comprehensive identity recovery.
Availability is not recoverability
When identity systems are compromised, misconfigured, or maliciously altered, the impact extends 
far beyond IT. Employees can lose access to critical applications, security policies may fail, automated 
workflows can break, and recovery efforts often become manual, time-consuming, and difficult to 
validate. 
This checklist will help you identify common gaps in identity resilience, recovery readiness, and 
operational protection across your IAM environment. 
1. Are your critical identity systems truly protected?
As identity environments become more interconnected and automated, the impact of a com-
promised admin account, configuration error, or malicious change can spread quickly across 
users, permissions, policies, and business-critical applications. Many organizations still rely 
on manual recovery processes with limited visibility into identity changes, increasing the risk 
of prolonged downtime, security gaps, and operational disruption when incidents occur. 
A strong identity resilience strategy helps reduce this risk through independent, point-in-
time backups stored outside the production environment. Teams can quickly recover users, 
groups, roles, conditional access policies, and MFA configurations without manual effort, 
enabling fast and reliable recovery after ransomware, administrative error, or other identity-
related incidents.
2. Could your organization recover from a compromised identity 
environment? 
Ransomware and identity-based attacks increasingly target privileged accounts, policies, 
and access configurations that organizations depend on to operate securely. As AI-
enhanced phishing, social engineering, and automated attacks become more sophisticated, 
unauthorized changes can spread rapidly across users, groups, permissions, and policies. 
If recovery points are compromised or backups can be altered, organizations may be 
left without a reliable path to clean recovery, increasing the risk of lockouts, operational 
disruption, and costly manual rebuilds.

3
© 2026 Keepit. All rights reserved
To strengthen resilience against malicious activity, identity backups should be immutable 
and isolated from the primary IAM environment. Teams should be able to quickly roll back 
unauthorized changes from compromised accounts and rely on tested recovery processes to 
restore identity data, policies, and configurations cleanly and consistently after ransomware 
or other cyber incidents.
3. How quickly could your identity environment recover from disruption?
During a cyber incident or administrative failure, slow and inconsistent recovery processes 
can quickly disrupt employee productivity, application access, and business operations. 
Many organizations still rely on manual scripts, fragmented recovery steps, or undocumented 
processes that make identity restoration difficult to execute under pressure. Limited recovery 
options and unclear recovery time objectives (RTOs) further increase the risk of delays, errors, 
and incomplete restores when rapid recovery matters most. 
Modern identity resilience requires recovery processes that are standardized, tested, and 
aligned to defined recovery time objectives. Teams should be able to quickly restore entire 
environments or recover specific users, groups, roles, and policies with precision, helping 
minimize downtime and maintain operational continuity during identity-related incidents.
4. Could you quickly recover from harmful policy or configuration 
changes?
Identity environments are constantly evolving, with policies, permissions, and access settings 
changing across users, applications, and administrative teams. Without clear visibility into 
historical configurations and the ability to quickly restore known-good settings, even small 
misconfigurations or unauthorized changes can create significant operational and security 
risk. As identity systems become more automated and interconnected, these issues can 
spread quickly, leading to access disruptions, policy drift, and security gaps that are difficult 
to identify and correct. 
Strong configuration and policy resilience helps teams maintain visibility into identity 
changes over time and recover quickly from accidental or malicious modifications. Historical 
versions of policies and settings can be compared, audited, and restored when needed, 
helping reduce operational disruption and maintain a stronger security posture.
5. Could you prove identity recoverability during an audit or investigation? 
As identity systems become more critical to business operations, maintaining clear 
records of identity changes, policy modifications, administrative activity, and recovery 
events is essential for both compliance and incident response. Many organizations still 
lack the visibility and reporting needed to support forensic investigations, demonstrate 
recoverability, or prove compliance with frameworks such as GDPR and SOC 2. During audits 
or security incidents, these gaps can delay response efforts, increase regulatory exposure, 
and create operational and reputational risk. 
Mature identity resilience strategies help reduce this exposure by preserving complete 
audit trails for users, groups, roles, policies, and administrative changes. Backup data can 
be retained in a way that supports legal hold requirements and forensic investigations, 
while recovery and audit reporting helps organizations demonstrate identity protection and 
recovery readiness with greater confidence and transparency.

4
6. Does your identity recovery strategy extend beyond native IAM 
protections?
Many organizations assume their IAM provider is fully responsible for protecting and 
recovering identity data, policies, and configurations. In reality, native protections are 
primarily designed for service availability, not comprehensive backup and recovery. 
Overreliance on retention policies, recycle bins, or limited rollback capabilities can leave 
critical gaps in identity resilience that often remain hidden until an incident occurs. 
A strong shared responsibility strategy recognizes that identity protection and recoverability 
are essential components of broader cyber resilience planning. Identity systems should be 
treated as Tier 0 infrastructure, with independent backup and recovery capabilities designed 
to protect users, groups, policies, configurations, and other critical identity data from 
operational failure, ransomware, or administrative error.
Now, assess your risk
Identity failures rarely start with a complete outage. More often, they begin with compromised 
accounts, configuration drift, administrative errors, or malicious changes that quietly spread across 
the environment before the impact is fully understood. 
Request a meeting with a Keepit resilience expert to identify potential gaps in identity recoverability, 
operational readiness, and cyber resilience across Microsoft Entra ID and Okta. 
Better understand where your organization may be exposed and validate your recovery readiness 
before an identity-related incident disrupts business operations.

ABOUT THIS EXCERPT 
The content for this excerpt was taken directly from IDC MarketScape: Worldwide SaaS 
Data Protection 2025–2026 Vendor Assessment (Doc # US52971725).  
IDC OPINION 
SaaS data protection remains one of the biggest challenges in the data protection 
market for vendors and buyers alike. 
Data protection vendors have long been able to provide backup and recovery for any 
application, running in any environment, on any storage. However, this breadth of 
coverage does not extend to every SaaS application. SaaS data protection is a 
subsection of the larger data protection market, and very few vendors are focused 
solely on providing data protection for SaaS applications. They must balance 
developing data protection capabilities with supporting the SaaS applications their 
customers demand. 
As a result, IT buyers face a market that can be described as top heavy. They can find 
many third-party products that can protect the most popular SaaS applications, but far 
fewer options for niche SaaS applications that aren't widely adopted or are industry 
specific. Buyers are put in the uncomfortable position of balancing using multiple SaaS 
data protection vendors, using the native data protection tools from the SaaS vendors 
themselves, internally developing their own method and workflow for exporting SaaS 
data for protection, or a combination of these to cover all their SaaS applications. 
It is, therefore, unlikely that a single, perfect SaaS data protection solution that will 
address every IT buyer's needs exists. However, by knowing what solutions are in the 
market and what criteria to consider, buyers can narrow the search for the best SaaS 
data protection solution for them. The purpose of this evaluation is to offer guidance to 
that end. 
This IDC MarketScape evaluates what we believe are the six most prominent SaaS data 
protection vendors. It is designed to help readers differentiate between these vendors' 
solutions and align their capabilities and features with their own organizational needs. 
IDC MARKETSCAPE VENDOR INCLUSION CRITERIA 
To narrow the list of participants to those we believe are most significant, we applied 
the following inclusion criteria:

©2025 IDC 
#US52971725e 
3 
▪ The vendor offers a purpose-built solution for at least five SaaS applications.  
▪ The vendor's solution will be considered in totality of "own IP" and "other IP" (i.e., 
partnerships), provided that at least 80% of the vendor's core solution is 
primarily "own IP."  
▪ The vendor's solution must be available as standalone products (options for 
inclusion as a bundle are acceptable). 
▪ The solution must be available in at least two of the three major geographies 
(NA, EMEA, APJ). 
▪ The core solution must have been in general market availability on January 1, 
2024, with all features under consideration in general availability as of May 31, 
2025. Features released after that time are considered road map items. 
Our goal was to facilitate a head-to-head assessment with enough latitude that each 
vendor can illustrate its unique value and not box vendors into a one-size-fits-all 
evaluation. 
ADVICE FOR TECHNOLOGY BUYERS 
IDC research found that for SaaS application data protection, most organizations use 
native tools from SaaS vendors. These tools often have limitations or require an 
additional license to unlock premium data protection capabilities. 
The vendors in this analysis can, at the bare minimum, provide greater value than what 
SaaS application vendors can natively supply, simply because they can protect multiple 
SaaS applications on a single platform. They often go beyond data backup and recovery 
and can provide long-term data retention, immutable data storage, ransomware 
protection, security, and other capabilities. 
SaaS data protection vendors differentiate themselves in several ways. Very often, 
these involve trade-offs. Some key considerations are: 
▪ Breadth of SaaS application coverage: Many organizations use multiple SaaS 
applications. Since most data protection vendors cover the most popular 
business applications, buyers may value vendors that support more niche SaaS 
applications they are using. 
▪ Depth of solution: Some vendors focus on specific capabilities to expand SaaS 
data protection beyond just backup and recovery. These often include 
compliance, cyber-resilience, and other capabilities. Buyers will need to consider 
what they need and balance that with the solution's breadth of SaaS application 
coverage.

©2025 IDC 
#US52971725e 
4 
▪ Data sovereignty: To remain compliant, buyers should pay attention to the data 
residency options that the SaaS data protection solution provides. Buyers should 
consider whether the solution is hosted in a public cloud, the vendor's private 
datacenters, or if there are options for customers to host the backup data in 
their own datacenters, especially if there are cross-region or cross-cloud failover 
capabilities involved. 
▪ Price: While price was not an evaluation criterion in this IDC MarketScape, it 
certainly is an issue for every buyer. Solutions mentioned in this document will 
vary by price, and it is up to buyers to find the balance between cost and solution 
capabilities. 
▪ SaaS application coverage road map: Many of the vendors in this evaluation 
publicly disclose the specific SaaS applications they intend to support as road 
map items, which can be helpful in choosing a solution. However, buyers should 
also consider vendors' expansion strategies because they may affect how long it 
will take for road map items to become generally available. 
This IDC MarketScape is best used as a way to identify solution differentiation and 
formulate a short list of vendor candidates for further consideration. 
We believe every vendor in this evaluation could be the perfect solution in some 
scenarios and less optimal in other scenarios. IT buyers are advised to use this 
document to narrow the field and then apply their own due diligence and proof-of-
concept prior to making any selection or purchase. 
VENDOR SUMMARY PROFILE 
This section briefly explains IDC's key observations resulting in a vendor's position in 
the IDC MarketScape. While every vendor is evaluated against each of the criteria 
outlined in the Appendix, the description here provides a summary of each vendor's 
strengths and challenges. 
Keepit 
IDC has identified Keepit as a Leader in this 2025–2026 IDC MarketScape for worldwide 
SaaS data protection vendor assessment. 
Keepit, headquartered in Denmark and founded in 2007, is a pure-play provider 
focused exclusively on backup and recovery for SaaS applications. Keepit delivers SaaS 
data protection through a vendor-neutral, API-driven platform with independent cloud 
infrastructure as its back end instead of a public cloud. The solution provides unified 
backup and recovery across all supported SaaS applications, which include Microsoft

©2025 IDC 
#US52971725e 
5 
365, Salesforce, Google Workspace, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Azure DevOps, Power 
Platform, and others. 
Data sovereignty is one of Keepit's core value propositions. All customer backup data is 
stored in independent, Keepit-owned datacenters located in multiple global regions, 
ensuring retention, residency, and compliance. The private cloud infrastructure also 
allows Keepit to offer unlimited data retention, predictable seat-based pricing, and no 
volume-based or egress fees. 
Key solution capabilities include cross-user and in-place restore, point-in-time 
snapshots, fast indexing with smart search and preview, a unified multi-SaaS 
management dashboard, anomaly detection, logical air-gapping, and multitenant 
management capabilities and white-labeling options specifically designed for MSPs. The 
platform also features proprietary object storage using blockchain-like (Merkle tree) 
immutability. 
Strengths 
▪ Vendor-independent cloud infrastructure: Keepit stores its customers' backup 
data in its own datacenters, which are located in Denmark, Switzerland, 
Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, and Australia. This 
ensures sovereign data control without relying on public cloud providers. 
▪ Blockchain-like immutability: All Keepit backups are stored in proprietary 
object storage using blockchain-like (Merkle tree) immutability. Once written, 
data cannot be overwritten, deleted, or modified until outside the customer's 
retention policy. 
▪ Direct data access: Backup data is stored outside the SaaS environment and 
can be accessed during SaaS outages for business continuity and data survival. 
Since it's stored on Keepit's cloud, there is no chance that data availability is 
impacted by public cloud outages. 
▪ Rapid onboarding for new SaaS applications: Keepit uses a proprietary 
Domain-Specific Language for rapid integration of new SaaS applications and has 
recently expanded coverage into Jira, Okta, Confluence, Docusign, and Miro. It 
will support GitHub and Monday.com in the near future. 
Challenges 
▪ SaaS data protection only: Keepit doesn't cover on-premises, VM, or container 
workloads, limiting its appeal to customers seeking all-in-one solutions. In 
addition, as a specialized vendor, it will face challenges competing against large 
enterprise backup vendors expanding into SaaS data protection. 
▪ Limited customer-premises/offline backup option: All backups remain in 
Keepit's dedicated cloud, which can be a dealbreaker for customers that are

©2025 IDC 
#US52971725e 
6 
mandated to keep backup copies in their own datacenters. Keepit allows 
scheduled export via physical media in special agreements to help address this. 
Consider Keepit When 
Keepit is a suitable choice for businesses that want a focused SaaS data protection 
vendor rather than a generalist backup provider encompassing multiple traditional IT 
workloads. Buyers for whom regulatory compliance and data sovereignty are top 
priorities or otherwise require backups to be on infrastructure outside major public 
clouds will also find Keepit appealing. 
APPENDIX 
Reading an IDC MarketScape Graph 
For the purposes of this analysis, IDC divided potential key measures for success into 
two primary categories: capabilities and strategies.  
Positioning on the y-axis reflects the vendor's current capabilities and menu of services, 
and how well aligned the vendor is to customer needs. The capabilities category 
focuses on the capabilities of the company and product today, here and now. Under 
this category, IDC analysts will look at how well a vendor is building/delivering 
capabilities that enable it to execute its chosen strategy in the market. 
Positioning on the x-axis, or strategies axis, indicates how well the vendor's future 
strategy aligns with what customers will require in three to five years. The strategies 
category focuses on high-level decisions and underlying assumptions about offerings, 
customer segments, and business and go-to-market plans for the next three to five 
years. 
The size of the individual vendor markers in the IDC MarketScape represents the 
annual SaaS data protection revenue of each individual vendor being assessed. It 
doesn't represent any other data protection revenue.  
For this 2025–2026 IDC MarketScape for worldwide SaaS data protection, capabilities 
were weighed more heavily than strategies to emphasize current market needs and the 
vendors currently addressing them. 
IDC MarketScape Methodology 
IDC MarketScape criteria selection, weightings, and vendor scores represent well-
researched IDC judgment about the market and specific vendors. IDC analysts tailor the 
range of standard characteristics by which vendors are measured through structured 
discussions, surveys, and interviews with market leaders, participants, and end users.

©2025 IDC 
#US52971725e 
7 
Market weightings are based on user interviews, buyer surveys, and the input of IDC 
experts in each market. IDC analysts base individual vendor scores, and ultimately 
vendor positions on the IDC MarketScape, on detailed surveys and interviews with the 
vendors, publicly available information, and end-user experiences in an effort to 
provide an accurate and consistent assessment of each vendor's characteristics, 
behavior, and capability. 
Market Definition 
While it is not itself a separate market, SaaS data protection capabilities are a subset of 
data protection software. Our definitions of pertinent market components follow: 
▪ Data protection software: Data protection software is focused on the 
protection, restoration, and recovery of data in the event of physical or logical 
errors. Products within the data protection and recovery market include data 
protection, continuous data protection (CDP), bare metal restore, 
backup/recovery software, host-based replication, and array-based replication 
(inclusive of snapshots, mirror/clones, and remote replication). Data protection 
software includes revenue from licensed software and online data protection 
services (aka online backup) licensed in a subscription fashion. This is inclusive of 
file- and image-level backup software, CDP software, and backup reporting 
software. 
▪ Data protection as a service: DPaaS is an umbrella term that includes backup, 
archive, disaster recovery, and cyber-recovery as a service. These are cloud-
based services fully managed by the service provider. Most DPaaS solutions can 
address on-premises, hybrid, and multicloud workloads. 
▪ Disaster recovery and disaster recovery as a service (DRaaS): Disaster 
recovery systems include all of the infrastructure, process management, and 
services necessary to restart an entire workload either on premises or in a public 
cloud environment. DRaaS differs from on-premises and traditional disaster 
recovery in that DRaaS is a cloud-based, fully managed service. An organization 
may declare a disaster response based on datacenter fires or broken water 
pipes, power loss, and regional events such as train derailments, plane crashes, 
or terror events, as well as earthquakes, floods, tornadoes, and hurricanes. 
▪ Cyber-recovery and cyber-recovery as a service (CRaaS): Cyber-recovery 
builds upon disaster recovery, and CRaaS builds upon DRaaS. Cyber-recovery in 
both contexts includes all infrastructure, process management, 
analytics/forensics, and professional services to assist organizations in 
recovering from malware attacks in general and ransomware specifically. To 
qualify as a CRaaS service, we believe it must include all of the components of 
DRaaS (in other words, the ability to reestablish an application workload in its

©2025 IDC 
#US52971725e 
8 
entirety) plus provisioning for a sanitary sandbox, forensic analysis, and curated 
recovery. Some vendors may go substantially beyond that with additional data 
security functions for added value and differentiation.

Synopsis 
This IDC study is an evaluation of six prominent SaaS data protection vendors on a 
worldwide basis and offers details on each vendor's capabilities and offerings. This 
evaluation is intended to help IT buyers differentiate between SaaS data protection 
solutions and narrow down candidates that fit their specific needs. 
"With so many SaaS applications, it is often difficult for organizations to find a data 
protection solution that offers both the breadth of SaaS application coverage to 
support everything they use and the depth of capabilities to make it more valuable 
than what native tools can do," said Johnny Yu, research manager, Infrastructure 
Software Platform at IDC. "This IDC MarketScape is designed to help IT buyers find that 
balance of breadth and depth and narrow down their choices of SaaS data protection 
solutions to ones that best match their needs."
