Executive summary
Intelligent data governance  |  4
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
“He who defends everything defends nothing.” 
This quote by Frederick the Great highlights the importance of prioritization, and now, 
centuries later, organizations continue to work with finite resources, and prioritization remains 
essential to ensuring those resources are optimally directed in support of strategies and 
desired outcomes.
A crucial enabler of prioritization for today’s digital-centric businesses is data and system 
classification: the process of separating and organizing data and systems into relevant groups 
based on shared characteristics, such as the level of sensitivity, risks presented, and privacy 
and protection requirements. Clear data and system classification enables organizations to:
•	Implement safeguards aligned with protection needs, such as those required by regulations (e.g., 
GDPR, NIS2, DORA, HIPAA, etc.), certifications, standards, and contracts
•	Define and execute comprehensive backup and recovery programs to improve resilience (i.e., 
prevention, detection, and recovery) against disruption or corruption — whether from a cyberattack 
or a more mundane cause
•	Safely and responsibly introduce new technologies and processes, including software-as-a-
service (SaaS) applications and cutting-edge AI capabilities
In fact, data classification is a necessary element of data governance, which consists 
of policies and standards intended to ensure the availability, quality, and security of an 
organization’s data. While data governance initiatives are often driven by applicable 
regulations and obligations, the benefits of such programs also include stronger business 
continuity and overall resilience, improved data accuracy and better outcomes based on that 
data (e.g., from day-to-day operations to breakthrough research), and greater data literacy 
and scale within the organization.
Rather than being perceived as burdensome overhead, data governance should be 
understood as a means to achieve highly desired outcomes more effectively and efficiently.
As CISOs and CIOs are responsible for supporting business continuity and enabling 
the business to innovate and advance, data governance programs typically fall on their 
shoulders. In collaboration with departments that own and use the organization’s data, 
and (ideally) with the support of the board, investors, and other senior executives, these IT 
leaders must adopt or develop a data governance framework that supports innovation while 
ensuring business continuity.
By doing so, CISOs and CIOs will create a strong foundation for their modern,  
data-driven enterprises.
I hope you find the report interesting. 
Kim Larsen
Keepit CISO
Executive summary

Introduction
02

Introduction
Intelligent data governance  |  6
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Today’s Chief Information Officers (CIOs) and Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) have 
two responsibilities that perhaps exist above all others:
1	 Support business continuity, by ensuring data and systems are available to the organization’s people, 
processes, and technologies and maintain adequate security levels
2	Enable the business to innovate and advance, by supporting research and development functions, 
including the introduction and adoption of new applications, workflows, and technologies
The thesis of this document is that because data is an essential component of these 
responsibilities — and therefore underpins both an organization’s biggest opportunities and 
biggest risks —  data governance should command serious attention and consideration.
In the context in which today’s organizations operate (see next page), such a statement may seem 
boring or even quaint. However, the operational reality is that data control is the prerequisite 
for practically everything an organization does or strives to do — including complying with 
regulations, contractual obligations, and even acquiring cyber insurance.
Where is your data? What data is important and why? Who has access to it?
Answering these questions is critically important, as without a clear understanding and mapping 
of your data, you can’t determine which processes and technologies to implement to preserve its 
availability, and you can’t responsibly, effectively, or efficiently innovate.
In the pages that follow, we’ll explore:
•	The importance of always-on data to today’s organizations
•	How to build resilience against data disruption and corruption
•	The foundational role of data governance in general, and data classification in particular
•	A practical approach to help you and your organization get started with data governance
Introduction

Introduction
Intelligent data governance  |  7
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
 
Cloud flexibility 
Most organizations have attempted to 
optimize workloads across public cloud, 
private data centers, and edge deployments.
 
 
 
 
SaaS adoption 
Organizations of all sizes have embraced 
software-as-a-service (SaaS) apps, but 
with this added convenience comes extra 
considerations for data protection and 
continuity planning.
 
The rise of AI 
Organizations are under pressure from 
investors and leaders to implement AI but 
must do so in a manner compliant with 
relevant laws and regulations governing data 
protection, privacy, and security (e.g., GDPR, 
HIPAA, PCI DSS, NIS2, DORA, etc.).
 
Interconnected risks 
Security, IT, compliance, and financial risks 
are increasingly interlinked, but regulatory 
frameworks remain siloed — forcing CISOs to 
develop unified risk management approaches 
while still mapping controls to specific 
regional requirements.
 
Budget pressures 
Cybersecurity and data governance may 
be seen as necessities, but budgets to 
implement and manage such programs 
remain limited — especially when they’re 
seen as costs rather than investments.
 
 
The broader context: 
Major trends shaping enterprise IT
To understand which challenges CIOs and CISOs are facing — and how they’re confronting 
them — Keepit conducted interviews with over 30 senior IT leaders across a range of 
industries. These in-depth conversations revealed key trends that serve as context for today’s 
enterprise IT organizations, including:

Key takeaways:
•	Data is ubiquitous in today’s organizations, and much of it is governed by regulations or is 
subject to other compliance obligations.
•	Data powers the present and creates the future, fueling day-to-day activities and serving 
as a critical input into innovation and improvement programs.
•	Maintaining access to uncorrupted data is essential and is one of the primary objectives 
of today’s CIOs and CISOs.
The importance of “always-on” data

Today’s organizations work with massive volumes of data in a wide range of forms, with 
some of the most common being:
•	Intellectual property including trade secrets, algorithms, business process details, source 
code, and customer lists
•	Internal and external communications, including text or chat messages, emails, voice calls,

Much of this data is subject to regulatory requirements pertaining 
to privacy and security that apply through the entire data lifecycle 
(see Figure 1, below).
Looking beyond regulations, many standards, certifications, 
and interoperability frameworks include similar requirements — 
particularly around access controls, secure storage, and secure transit.
From creation to deletion: The data lifecycle

The importance of “always-on” data
Intelligent data governance  |  10
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
While data lifecycle models differ in the details, they generally begin (from an 
organization’s perspective) with data’s creation or acquisition and end with its 
permanent deletion. 
We won’t dwell on the lifecycle too much, but instead will simply make a few points.
As noted, data can be:
•	Created: Some combination of human and machine effort generates new data, typically 
with data serving as an input to the process; or
•	Acquired: The organization comes into possession of data (e.g., a customer provides their 
information or completes a survey, the organization purchases or subscribes to a data 
source, equipment or applications produce telemetry, etc.).
Once acquired, data needs to be stored, with consideration given to:
•	Regulatory (and similar) requirements;
•	Cybersecurity concerns;
•	Accessibility; and
•	Availability (including redundancy and restoration capabilities).
Complicating matters, today’s IT environments include complex combinations of 
public and private clouds, SaaS applications, and on-premises infrastructure, as well 
as local storage on devices such as laptops and mobile phones. Add into this mix the 
rapid rise of AI — with its well-documented appetite for training and production data — 
and the unknowns associated with shadow IT, and it’s easy to see why “data sprawl” is a 
growing concern for IT leaders.
Next, data is put to use. In a moment, we’ll examine this stage in slightly more detail, but 
for now we’ll emphasize that understanding, establishing, and enforcing rules about 
which entities (e.g., people, devices, applications, and other systems) can access 
which data, for what purposes, is an important aspect of data governance. Moreover, 
not all users of an organization’s data are within that organization, as contractors, 
partners, vendors, and other external service providers also need controlled access.
At some point, data may no longer be needed for daily operations, or it may require 
deletion due to legal, regulatory, or compliance mandates, such as GDPR’s ‘Right 
to Be Forgotten.’ While some data can be deleted, other data must be retained for 
regulatory or business reasons. Regardless of the retention period, organizations 
should regularly test their backup and recovery processes to ensure that critical data 
remains accessible and intact when needed.
Finally, data that has no purpose or value — or that is subject to strict timelines 
governing how long it can be held — is permanently deleted. In the past, many 
organizations elected to retain data as long as possible “just in case”; however, in 
the contemporary climate of headline-grabbing data breaches and ever-stricter 
regulations, unnecessarily retaining data is regarded as introducing risk and liability.

Usage: Putting data to work
Let’s now circle back to the usage stage of the data lifecycle to illustrate how data 
is the lifeblood nurturing both an enterprise’s day-to-day operations and future 
aspirations.
Data powers the present
Typically, only a fraction of an organization’s resources is focused on the future; in most 
cases, considerably more attention is given to the processes, decisions, actions, and 
other activities that comprise day-to-day operations. In today’s digital businesses, 
data plays a vital role in
•	Communication utilities (e.g., email, instant messaging)
•	Collaboration platforms (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams)
•	Enterprise software suites
•	Domain- and industry-specific applications
•	Operational technology (OT), including industrial controllers and sensors
•	IT infrastructure
•	Customer relationship management (CRM) and customer data platforms (CDPs)
•	Human resources management (HRM) software
•	Inventory and production management software
•	Accounting, payroll, and other financial management software
•	SaaS applications (according to BetterCloud, the average company has deployed 103 SaaS 
apps, and the average enterprise has deployed 158.)
•	…and many others
What’s more, internal processes and technologies are remarkably interconnected, 
so a disruption in any one area has the potential to create ripples — some small, some 
significant, some truly disastrous — throughout the rest of the organization.
Data determines the future
A complete focus on today is a surefire way to become irrelevant 
tomorrow. Consequently, as their roles continue to evolve, CISOs 
and CIOs will be defined by their ability to enable and protect the 
innovation that’s so critical to an organization’s future.
Notably, innovation comes in multiple forms, including creating 
net new things (e.g., a research and development program) and 
finding more effective and efficient ways to do the things already 
being done.

In practice, innovation relies upon some mix of people, processes, and technology —

•	Few organizations do everything in house, with most make use of contractors, vendors,

Key takeaways:
•	There are three aspects to data resilience:  
(1) Preventing disruptions, (2) detecting problems, and (3) recovering to a safe state as quickly as 
possible, should a disruption occur.
•	Cyberattacks grab headlines, but account for only a small fraction of outages:  
Leaders shouldn’t overlook much more common causes, including misconfigurations, technical faults/
failures, natural disasters, contractual disputes, and human error.
•	Backup and recovery should be considered crucial components of operational hygiene:  
An emergency or other moment of desperation is not a good time to discover that processes or 
technologies aren’t performing as needed.
Resilience against data 
loss and corruption
As we’ve seen, today’s organizations rely on data. While responsibility is largely delegated, leaders, 
including the CIO and CISO, are ultimately accountable for ensuring data resilience — so that users, 
applications, and other entities can access the data stores as needed.
Resilience itself has three primary components:
•	Prevention: Technological and procedural mechanisms maintain uptime and guard against corruption, 
inadvertent deletion, and unauthorized access.
•	Detection: The ability to identify (as quickly as possible) outages, malicious or accidental changes, 
unauthorized access, and other problems or threats.
•	Recovery: In the event that disruption occurs, ensuring that the organization has and is able to execute the 
processes, supported by technology solutions, to restore data access as quickly and completely as possible.
Prevention is largely about robust IT architecture, redundant connectivity, identity and access 
management (IAM), and service level agreements (SLAs) with vendors, while detection leverages 
technical measures including real-time alerts and log monitoring.
For the purposes of this document, we’ll presume that IT leaders have such matters covered. 
Recovery, though, deserves some attention.
What causes data outages?
Cyberattacks garner headlines and cyber defense is rightfully 
becoming a board-level issue, but leaders shouldn’t let the threat of 
adversary-associated outages distract from other common causes.
For broad perspective, we can look to Splunk’s  “The hidden costs 
of downtime” which states that downtime stems from two main 
sources: 56% from security incidents (e.g., phishing attacks), while

and costly

company sees 466 hours 
of cybersecurity-related

© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
44% comes from app or infrastructure issues (e.g., software failures). In both cases, 
human error is the leading cause and the hardest to detect and remediate.
Data outages are likely to be caused by a handful of comparatively mundane issues 
(each of which has many underlying contributors, including human error):
•	Power: 44%
•	Network: 14%
•	IT systems (hardware, software): 13%
•	Cooling: 13%
•	Third-party provider: 8%
For example, in May 2024, UniSuper (an Australian superannuation fund managing 
$135 billion for 647,000 members) faced an unprecedented crisis when their entire 
Google Cloud account — including backups — was suddenly gone, the result of 
a misconfiguration within Google Cloud’s system. This “one-of-a-kind event,” as 
described by Google, wiped out UniSuper’s cloud subscription and its backups stored 
across multiple geographic locations. The result was a nearly two-week outage that 
left members without access to their accounts. Fortunately, UniSuper had maintained 
additional backups with an independent third-party provider, which proved to be the 
saving grace and played a crucial role in the recovery process.
More widely known, though, is the massive outage that began in July 2024, when 
cybersecurity company CrowdStrike rolled out a faulty update to their Falcon Sensor 
security software. Worldwide, approximately 8.5 million Windows systems crashed 
and could not be properly restarted, resulting in what has been called the largest 
outage in the history of IT as organizations struggled to restore systems and the data 
they housed.
So, while CIOs and CISOs should definitely champion a strong 
security posture, care must be taken not to overlook the more 
prosaic everyday risks.
Bringing backup to the forefront
Because few developments have the potential to stop an 
organization in its tracks — and to keep it stopped — like a data 
outage, the ability to recover critical systems should never be left 
to assumptions or chance.
Rather, the organization’s backup and recovery preparedness 
should be elevated from “IT concerns” to board-level 
considerations, alongside other operational resilience, business 
continuity, and compliance matters.

Intelligent data governance  |  16
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
In fact, compliance could be an effective way to bring backup to the forefront. For 
example, for those organizations subject to European Union’s NIS2 Directive, achieving 
compliance is likely a high-priority project, with regular reporting to the executive 
ranks. But how many executive teams know that Article 21 of the NIS2 Directive sets out 
clear cybersecurity risk-management measures “to protect network and information 
systems” that focus on ensuring business continuity through “backup management 
and disaster recovery.”
How many understand that with the NIS2 Directive, the governance provisions are 
tightened so that the responsibility for violation is not only imposed on the legal entity 
but on the management itself?
And NIS2 is hardly an exception when it comes to these (and similar) obligations, so 
such concerns aren’t limited to organizations based in or operating in the EU.
Moreover, backup and recovery must be understood as being more than just creating 
copies of data for future access. Are the copies secure? Is the data within backup 
repositories immutable? Are the repositories accessible, and is that access itself 
redundant? What are the different procedures for recovering different systems?
Even such basic questions as these can open hearts and minds to the subject’s 
complexities and subtleties — and the more that executives understand backup and 
recovery, the more resources will be made available to the CIOs and CISOs looking to 
protect the organization.
Training and testing for resilience
Too often, backup systems and recovery processes have been 
managed with a “set it and forget it” approach in which the 
organization selects and implements one or more solutions, 
defines and validates some recovery processes, and then largely 
ignores the subject except for periodic and fairly superficial 
checks.
But this hope-for-the-best approach just isn’t good enough — for 
your organization or for regulators. Rather, it takes a combination 
of training and testing to build, maintain, refine, and validate your 
ability to recover following a data loss or corruption event.
Training is intended to ensure that each member of your team 
knows their responsibilities within the recovery processes, so that 
decisions can be made and workflows can be executed quickly 
and efficiently.
Monkeying around
Chaos engineering is the 
practice of intentionally 
creating faults and unforeseen 
scenarios within a system to 
test (and ultimately improve) its 
resilience.
While the discipline’s origins 
date to (at least) development 
of the first Apple Macintosh in 
1983, chaos engineering gained 
new prominence in 2011 with 
Netflix’ Chaos Monkey tool.
To be clear, we aren’t 
suggesting you should 
randomly disable systems or 
embrace anarchy; however, 
we are adamant that the more 
exercises you conduct (from 
small disruptions to “extinction-
level” events), the more resilient 
your organization will be.

Resilience against data loss and corruption
Intelligent data governance  |  17
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Testing ensures that data recovery is possible in the event of a real crisis. Testing should 
cover full recovery (i.e., not simply confirming that backup copies exist) and should be 
applied to the full range of data and systems an organization might need to restore. 
After all, an emergency is not the time to discover that there’s an issue with a particular 
restoration process or that a critical SaaS system has changed how it ingests data.
Of course, CIOs and CISOs operate in a world of limited resources, which imposes 
the need for prioritization. In the context of backup and recovery, prioritization means 
answering questions like:
•	Which data is most important to our operations?
•	What systems need to be restored first?
•	What are our compliance (and similar) obligations?
Such questions aren’t limited to the scope of backup and recovery — they’re also a part 
of data governance.
Guidelines: Testing backup and recovery
Ensuring the effectiveness of your backup and disaster recovery processes is crucial for 
maintaining data integrity and business continuity. Put simply, the more direct, hands-on 
experience your team has in this regard, the better prepared they’ll be to swiftly recover 
critical data in diverse, pressure-packed, real-world scenarios.
Here are key steps to follow while testing your capabilities:
1	 Validate restoration capability promptly: Promptly validate that your backup systems can 
efficiently restore critical data without compromising integrity. 
2	 Determine acceptable downtime: Establish the maximum allowable time for data recovery, 
aligning with recovery time objectives set during prioritization.
3	 Regularly test backups for confidence: Frequently test your backups to instill confidence in 
your disaster recovery plan and promptly address any identified issues.
4	 Consider different scenarios: Simulate diverse scenarios, testing the recovery of individual 
files, entire databases, and complete systems to identify weaknesses.
5	 Document and analyze results: After each testing session, document and analyze the time, 
accuracy, and challenges encountered to gain insights for improvement.
6	 Involve relevant stakeholders: Collaborate with IT teams, data custodians, and business 
continuity managers to ensure comprehensive testing aligns with broader goals.
7	 Update and improve: Continuously update recovery plans based on testing insights, addressing 
weaknesses, refining procedures, and adapting to evolving threats.
Diligently adhering to the rigorous testing guidelines outlined above paves the way for a 
robust IT compliance policy and serves as proactive measures against evolving cyberthreats.

Key takeaways:
•	Data governance is an investment in the business: Effective data governance supports 
business continuity and resilience, impacts any and all outcomes based on data, guards 
against compliance failures, and improves the organization’s ability to work with data.
•	Data classification is the foundation of data governance: Creating and leveraging a data 
governance framework begins with a data classification standard.
•	Data classification is a team effort: Leaders establish and champion effective governance 
and delegate classification to data owners; data owners collaborate with data users to 
determine prioritization.
•	Modern tooling can lessen the burden of data classification:AI-powered data 
classification solutions help to categorize existing data, keep up with new data, and 
enable automation of data-centric processes.

The foundational role of 
data governance
Existing under the broad umbrella of data management, 
data governance is a program — implemented via policies 
and standards — intended to ensure the availability, 
quality, and security of an organization’s data, in 
accordance with applicable regulations and obligations 
(e.g., contractual commitments, adhering to industry 
standards, fulfilling requirements for certifications, etc.).
Within data governance, data classification is the process 
of separating and organizing data into relevant groups 
(“classes”) based on shared characteristics, such as 
the level of sensitivity, risks presented, and privacy and 
protection requirements.
As we will now see, data governance in general and data 
classification in particular are essential foundations of the 
modern, data-driven enterprise.
Data governance as an investment
An effective data governance program delivers several beneficial outcomes.
First, by helping to ensure the availability, quality, and security of an 
organization’s data, data governance is a pillar of organizational and business 
continuity and overall resilience.

The foundational role of data governance
Intelligent data governance  |  20
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Second, because data governance helps improve overall data accuracy, it also impacts 
outcomes based on that data — which can range from comparatively simple day-to-day 
business decisions and operations to more complex, forward-looking initiatives including 
research and development, automation, and AI-focused programs.
Third, by supporting the organization’s efforts to comply with regulations and other 
obligations, data governance helps to avoid both the direct consequences of failing to 
comply and the negative outcomes that regulations, standards, contracts, and similar 
obligations are intended to guard against.
Finally, an effective data governance program permeates the entire organization, increasing 
data literacy and contributing to improved data scale. Along with data quality, and the 
confidence that comes with knowing data is being handled in a manner that respects privacy 
and ensures its security, these factors act as a rising tide that levels-up all of the organization’s 
data-related capabilities.
Data classification: The foundation of data governance
An organization’s resources are finite and must be deployed in alignment with priorities. In 
a data governance context, this means that organizations must begin by establishing and 
implementing a foundation of data (and system) classification.
To protect sensitive data and support the continuity of systems and processes that depend 
on it, data must be located, classified according to its level of sensitivity, and accurately 
tagged. Then, enterprises must handle each group of data in ways that ensure only authorized 
people (both internal and external) can gain access, and that the data is always handled in 
compliance with relevant regulations.
To create a data classification strategy, information is divided into predefined groups that 
share a common risk (see Figure 3, below), and the corresponding security controls required 
to secure each group type are identified.

Delegation in data classification 
Understanding the nature of your data is key to strengthening your organization’s data 
resilience.
Whether safeguarding CEO emails, logistics data, customer information, intelligence 
dashboards, or proprietary code, identifying the priority for recovery establishes 
a strategic foundation — speeding up recovery and ensuring that your business 
continuity efforts are precisely aligned with the specific datasets crucial for sustaining 
your operations.
While upper management has an important role to play in championing data 
governance and, in some jurisdictions, is legally responsible for regulatory violations, 
assigning prioritization should be delegated to the departments that actually own and 
manage different subsets of the organization’s data.
It is these owners who, in close collaboration with the users and consumers of data, 
must make the tough calls about the relative importance of different datasets, thereby 
forming the basis for strategic prioritization. 
Modern data classification and AI-powered tools
When done correctly, data classification makes using and 
protecting data easier and more efficient and becomes the 
foundation for critical data governance strategies and the driver 
for broad security controls.
However, because the process can seem burdensome and 
intimidating, there can be a tendency for organizations to ‘drag 
their feet’ on this important initiative.
Fortunately, classification tools — especially those powered by 
modern AI technologies — can significantly lessen the burdens 
associated with helping to discover your data and create scalable 
classification processes and systems.
Plus, these tools can also help with day-to-day adherence to 
data classification guidelines, by automating the treatment and 
handling of sensitive data and by promoting a culture of security 
that increases awareness of data sensitivity and prevents the 
storing of sensitive content on removable media or third-party 
web portals.
AI considerations
AI offers powerful capabilities for automation, analysis, and efficiency, but it also 
comes with risks, including data integrity challenges, evolving cyberthreats, and 
unpredictable system behavior. Human intelligence is still essential for the successful 
implementation of data and classification systems. 
 
AI should be viewed and used as an assistant — not a decision-maker. AI-driven tools 
should be implemented with a strong focus on security, compliance, and user control. 
It is essential to ensure that AI does not alter or manipulate critical data in unintended 
ways. As AI continues to evolve, responsible adoption requires transparency, rigorous 
testing, and safeguards that protect data while enabling innovation and resilience.

Key takeaways:
•	Tap into the board of directors and investors: Foster an ongoing relationship, including 
agenda time during board meetings, by aligning with business objectives, translating 
technical concepts, demonstrating ROI, and seeking board feedback and support.
•	Mix and match from existing frameworks to create something that works for your 
organization: Many frameworks exist, but finding one that fits your needs can be a major 
challenge; instead, review what’s available and adopt a structure that meets today’s needs 
and can be adapted or extended as your organization evolves.
•	Find and classify your data: Don’t let perfect be the enemy of good enough — three or four 
classification categories are usually sufficient and won’t overwhelm the departments and 
personnel whose support is crucial for the program’s success.
A practical approach to governance
Sound data governance depends on adopting a precise — yet practical — framework for consistent 
data handling across the organization.
To help you choose which path is best for your organization, and to maximize your success on the data 
governance journey, we offer the following guidance.
Engaging leadership in governance
Fostering a culture of awareness and accountability at the highest levels of leadership builds trust 
with stakeholders and, in the long run, better protects your organization’s assets.
Ideally, CISOs, CIOs, and other IT leaders can earn the opportunity to involve and update board 
members periodically — even if only for 15 minutes of a board meeting. To do so, we recommend:
•	Aligning with business objectives: Frame data governance discussions in the context of the company’s 
overall business objectives and risk tolerance. Highlight the impact of data governance on key business 
functions, financial performance, and reputation.
•	Translate technical concepts: When discussing or presenting data governance concepts, adopt terminology 
and leverage examples that can be easily understood by board members who may not have a technical 
background. Focus on the importance of data governance as a business enabler and risk mitigation measure, 
rather than as a purely technical issue or compliance checkbox.
•	Demonstrate ROI: Clearly articulate the return on investment (ROI) of data governance initiatives by 
quantifying the potential cost savings, risk reductions, and business benefits associated with effective 
classifications and controls. Use case studies and risk-impact metrics to illustrate the tangible impact of 
investments or potential costs of inaction.
•	Seek board feedback and support: Solicit feedback from board members on data governance strategy, 
priorities, and challenges. Leverage board members’ experience, expertise, and networks to garner support 
for governance initiatives and resource allocation.

10 questions for board discussions
To prepare for involving the board and investors in data governance discussions,  
ask and answer these questions:
What is the current level of understanding and engagement of our board members regarding data 
governance?
How frequently are cybersecurity, business continuity, compliance, and other subjects related to 
data governance discussed in board meetings?
What risk scenarios, analogies, or case studies should we present to the board to illustrate the 
business implications of data governance?
What specific topics or areas of concern do executive leadership and board members have about 
data governance and areas it impacts?
How can we effectively translate technical data governance concepts into business language that 
resonates with board members?
What educational sessions or materials can we provide to enhance board members’ 
understanding of data governance and closely related matters?
What is our current level of investment in data governance, and how does it compare to industry 
benchmarks?
What are the potential cost savings, risk reductions, and business benefits associated with our 
data governance initiatives?
What mechanisms can we establish for ongoing communication and collaboration between IT 
leaders and the board?
How can we leverage board members’ experience, expertise, and networks to support data 
governance initiatives?
 
Finding a governance framework 
Successful data governance requires rapid adoption of a chosen framework. Ideally, 
the framework is sufficiently precise and practical that it becomes the structure 
around which stakeholders will collaborate to ensure data is handled consistently 
across the organization.
However, getting started with data governance can feel overwhelming — especially 
if it’s your first foray into the field or if your organization has paid little attention to the 
subject until now.
The good news is that there are many existing options from which to choose, including:
•	The Data Governance Institute’s Data Governance Framework
•	DAMA International’s Data Management Body of Knowledge
•	Frameworks from Eckerson Group, PwC, and Deloitte

A practical approach to data governance
Intelligent data governance  |  25
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
But the less good news is that one of the top challenges reported to us by interviewed leaders is 
identifying and adopting an appropriate data governance framework that fits their organization.
For example, a framework has to be comprehensive enough to meet your organization’s needs but 
shouldn’t extend so far that it imposes work that has little or no practical purpose beyond simply 
adhering to the framework.
Similarly, a framework should be robust, but not so rigid that it can’t be extended to new pipelines 
and processes that emerge as your organization evolves.
For most organizations, the best (i.e., most practical, efficient, and effective) approach is to 
balance a set of fundamental elements common to existing frameworks with additional guidance 
introduced for specific applications and workflows.
10 questions to guide framework choices
To help find the framework that’s right for your organization,  
start by asking these questions:
How should data governance support our organization’s decision-making processes and reduce 
operational inefficiencies?
What governance structures (e.g., data governance council, data stewards) do we need to 
establish to oversee data governance efforts?
What policies and standards do we need to develop to govern data effectively (e.g., data 
classification, data quality, data privacy) and how can they consistently be applied and adhered to 
across the organization?
How will our data governance framework help us comply with relevant regulations and industry 
standards (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, etc.) — and how will we monitor and respond to changes 
in the regulatory landscape?
Is there an existing data governance framework that aligns well with our organization’s goals and 
existing data management practices?
If no framework is a particularly good fit, then what elements from existing frameworks can be 
adopted — and what gaps remain?
How will we identify and address challenges as we implement our chosen framework?
What roles and responsibilities should be assigned to different stakeholders within the 
organization to ensure clear ownership and accountability across various departments?
What processes will we implement to review and update policies and standards regularly?
How will we train and educate employees about our data governance framework and their roles 
in the governance process — and how will we measure the effectiveness of our training and 
awareness efforts?

A practical approach to data governance
Intelligent data governance  |  26
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Creating a classification strategy
Establishing effective data governance frameworks 
requires precise, practical data classification. In fact, this 
classification work sets the stage for everything else by 
forming the foundation for critical data governance that 
ultimately makes it easier to use and protect data.
Organizational buy-in is essential, as developing data 
classification models, compliance controls, and other 
framework elements is labor intensive and requires timely 
and informed input from data owners in various departments.
10 questions for classification strategy
To help plan and execute your data classification strategy,  
start by asking these questions:
What are the primary objectives of our data classification strategy, and how do they align with our 
overall data governance framework?
What types of data do we collect, store, and process, and where is this data located?
How sensitive is the data we handle, and what are the potential risks associated with unauthorized 
access or disclosure?
How does data classification support our compliance with industry regulations and standards 
(e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, etc.) — and how do we ensure ongoing compliance as relevant 
regulations and industry standards evolve?
What are the key business functions that rely on accurate data classification, how are they 
impacted by our classification strategy, and what is their expected (and agreed upon) level of 
involvement?
What predefined groups or categories will we use for data classification (e.g., Public, Internal only, 
Confidential, Restricted)?
What processes and procedures will we implement to classify data according to its sensitivity and 
importance?
How will we ensure that each data category has the appropriate security controls and access 
restrictions? How will we tag and label classified data to facilitate proper handling and protection?
What tools and technologies are available to support our data classification efforts, and how will 
we evaluate and select data classification tools?
What metrics and KPIs will we use to monitor the effectiveness of our data classification strategy?
DATA GOVERNANCE TIP
If your organization is beginning 
its data classification journey 
without a platform or tool, resist 
the urge to get too granular, as 
granular classification schemes 
tend to cause confusion and 
become unmanageable.
For most organizations, three to 
four classification categories are 
usually sufficient, and will allow 
your data governance initiatives 
to get off to a strong start.

Conclusion
Intelligent data governance  |  28
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved
Data sits at the center of both the biggest risks and the biggest opportunities facing 
organizations. CISOs and CIOs are responsible for safeguarding data with robust protections 
while also ensuring it’s available — in the right forms, to the right people, at the right time — to 
power both day-to-day operations and innovation initiatives.
Rather than being perceived as burdensome overhead, data governance should be 
understood as a means to achieve these desired outcomes more effectively and efficiently.
Ideally working with the support of the board, investors, and senior executives, and 
collaborating closely with the departments that own and use the organization’s data, it falls to 
CISOs and CIOs to champion and lead the data governance programs that are foundations of 
the modern, data-driven enterprise.
But data governance is not possible without data classification. The categories and 
other labels assigned to the organization’s data are critical for ensuring it is stored and 
used appropriately (whether for mundane tasks or breakthrough research). These same 
classifications also help to inform a reliable backup and restoration program — something that 
isn’t merely important for business continuity but is increasingly required by regulations.
Next steps: Finding a trusted partner
Given that data is central to both opportunities and risks, finding a trusted data protection 
partner is key — especially one that can offer robust and scalable data protection solutions 
tailored to your company’s needs.

for your most business-critical applications and platforms. Importantly, our approach goes 
beyond providing tools — we collaborate with you to implement best practices, stay ahead of 
emerging threats, and continuously improve your data governance strategies.
By partnering with Keepit, your organization can confidently navigate the complexities of 
today’s evolving cybersecurity challenges and regulatory requirements with a modern solution 
that ensuring data is secure, compliant, and ready to support innovative business initiatives.

please visit us at keepit.com.

Information security has never been more

systems—have migrated from on-prem-
ises appliances and servers to third-party 
cloud environments.

enterprises require, but it also introduces 
new challenges. Perhaps foremost among 
these issues, but one of the least-recog-
nized, is a shared data responsibility model 
and its important implications for business 
continuity planning, in general, and disas-
ter recovery specifically.

The 3-2-1 principle of backup (Figure 2) 
mandates that you must have one copy 
of your data off site. In the days of tape 
backup, where fire and theft were the only 
credible threats to your backup data, the 
off-site copy effectively ensured that your 
backup data would survive any calamity 
that could befall your primary data and 
your primary site.
In the cloud age, however, backups have 
become much more complicated: geo-
graphic dispersal is insufficient to ensure 
your data is secure, and hidden risks are 
introduced by relying on clouds that may 
be taken offline to protect the providers’ 
primary business interests.

True backup requires 
a separate logical 
infrastructure
While the requirement for separate backup 
infrastructure may seem self-evident to 
many IT and security professionals, most 
alternative cloud backup solutions will read-
ily store your backup directly on the same 
cloud infrastructure that hosts your primary 
data—introducing unnecessary risk and 
really stretching the meaning of “backup.” 
You can choose to store your backup data in 
the public cloud, and you can even specify 
a data center location that is separate from 
your primary data—but in no way does this 
approach provide the assurances that you 
need, because all your data (now including 
your only backups!) is managed under the 
same administrative infrastructure. ▶

﻿
Leading SaaS data security |  8
Consequently, if that infrastructure is com-
promised, then both your primary data and 
your backups are at risk, no matter if they 
reside on servers in different parts of the 
country or even on different continents.
In our view, offering “true backup” means 
guaranteeing to our customers that their 
backup data doesn’t reside on the same 
logical infrastructure as their primary data, 
regardless of which combination of prima-
ry workloads are being protected.
“True backup requires a 
logical infrastructure separate 
from the primary data”

stored on the same cloud infrastructure 
that hosts your primary data (e.g., Ama-
zon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, etc.), 
Keepit does not run on public cloud infra-
structure; instead, The Keepit Cloud:
•	 runs in our own data center regions
•	 operates on our own hardware 
•	 is managed by our own people
To ensure data sovereignty, once a cus-
tomer chooses a Keepit region for backup, 
their data never leaves that region. Not 
only does Keepit guarantee that backup 
data will always go to that region, but no 
processes exist that even could transfer 
backup data out of that region (aside from 
customer initiated restores and down-
loads, of course). ■

Leading SaaS data security |  12
Assuming physical security is adequate, 
no threat actor can erase the data stored 
on an offline tape. In the cloud, however, 
everything is always online and expecta-
tions for ease of use dictate a high degree 
of accessibility.
To ensure security while maintaining con-
venience, Keepit combines several protec-
tive measures (Table 1).
Protective measure
Benefits
Immediate encryption
Upon ingestion by the Keepit platform, backup data is immediately encrypted before it is written 
to storage media. This process employs industry best practice algorithms believed to offer 
unbreakable security for at least the next 30 years. 
30-day delete lock
There is no simple way to immediately delete your data in Keepit: you, or the attacker who has 
successfully taken over your identity, will have to wait for 30 days for datasets to be deleted or for 
accounts to be closed.
This deliberate delay is the first line of defense against user error, insider threats, and ransomware 
attacks that target backups.4 
Data region sovereignty 
and dual data center 
redundancy
To comply with data sovereignty requirements and desires for geographical dispersal of information 
assets, Keepit offers multiple regions around the world. Once your data enters a given Keepit region, 
your data stays in that region - forever.
To provide protection from the most common disasters such as fire, power or cooling system 
outages—or other events that can render a building or complex of buildings unusable—all data is 
copied into two separate data center facilities within the chosen region. 
Unique, tamper-proof 
infrastructure
The Keepit infrastructure runs on software that was designed and built from the ground up by our 
team. This proprietary storage infrastructure allows us to provide fast and reliable backup at a 
reasonable cost, and supports the data immutability that protects backup datasets—like the backup 
tapes of yesteryear, our disk-based storage systems do not offer a mechanism for modifying backup 
data.
This core characteristic means that even in a nightmare scenario—e.g., administrative accounts are 
compromised, primary data is corrupted or encrypted, attackers gain access to your backups—there 
is no way for the system to comply with an attacker’s efforts to tamper with your backup. 
4. Many ransomware families are adept at targeting backups. A recent study found that 94% of

Leading SaaS data security |  13
Architectural element
Benefits
Merkle Tree architecture
The Keepit information architecture is inspired by the Merkle tree structure that gained renown from 
blockchain systems such as Bitcoin and the ‘git’ version control system.
In addition to providing benefits including strong consistency checks, this design also allows us to 
represent and access backup sets over time—completely removing the antiquated model of ‘full’ and 
‘incremental’ backups, along with all the overhead associated with that legacy approach. 
“Incremental forever” data 
transfer
In the Keepit data model, when a backup executes, we effectively only transfer the differences in your 
dataset; however, when you view your data in the Keepit platform, all access is instant across time and 
space, and every single backup—no matter how old—appears as if it was a standalone full copy of 
your dataset at the time it was taken. 
 
We have even gone a step further: by designing, completely from scratch, an object storage 
architecture for this information model, we are able to store backup data very efficiently on simple 
high-density hard drive-based storage systems, which simplifies our supply chain and lowers both 
the risk and the price point for our customers. 
Secure, reliable and 
change-based long-
term data storage
We designed the Keepit platform for the 
specific purpose of providing secure and 
reliable long-term storage for SaaS backup 
data. In pursuit of this objective, we created 
a uniquely powerful information architecture 
(Table 2) that employs a Merkle tree struc-
ture and an innovative “incremental forever” 
approach to deliver performance and cost 
benefits that would simply not be possible 
on general-purpose storage services.
Table 2—By rethinking information architecture, the Keepit platform provides secure and reliable long-
term backup with unmatched performance

Leading SaaS data security |  16
Physical security
As noted in Table 1, once backup data 
reaches the Keepit platform, it is immedi-
ately copied into systems in two separate 
data centers within the designated region. 
This practice provides resilience in case a 
facility is permanently lost (e.g., to fire or a 
natural disaster) and also ensures contin-
uous availability of data in case of a more 
benign facility problem (e.g., temporary 
failure of power or cooling systems).
In every region, the Keepit platform oper-
ates in active-active mode between the 
two data centers. This model:
•	 Allows the platform to continue virtually un-
interrupted in the unlikely scenario that a full 
building is incapacitated
•	 Provides system-level redundancy, allowing 
the platform to continue servicing customers 
in case any single system is lost or needs to be 
taken offline for service, upgrades, mainte-
nance, or repairs
This system-level redundancy is comple-
mented by significant component-level 
redundancy on the individual servers that 
host the Keepit platform. Components 
that most commonly fail on modern serv-
ers (e.g., cooling fans, power supplies 
and spinning disks) can typically be hot 
swapped without even powering down the 
system holding the failed component.
Figure 7 - Each region has dual data centers which 
typically holds the above certifications.
While there are some local differences be-
tween the regions 5, all data center facilities 
employed by Keepit must conform to a 
physical security baseline that:
•	 Ensures high availability
•	 Restricts access to the physical systems that 
constitute the Keepit platform
Physical security at a facility can feature 
a combination of multi-factor authenti-
cation including biometric identification 
for facility access, controlled access with 
man traps, CCTV monitoring of the facility 
and facility perimeter, plus onsite security 
staff. Typically, the processing facilities will 
hold an ISO 27001 certification and several 
complementary certifications such as 
SOC-2, ISAE 3402, PCI/DSS, HIPAA etc.
When providing large-scale storage, failure 
of storage media is a regular and undra-
matic event. Failed storage media is never 
sent back to the media vendor for analysis; 
instead, it is kept onsite for physical disin-
tegration (mechanical shredding) before 
being disposed of, upholding Keepit’s 
commitment that customer data never 
leaves its designated region.
Additionally, and as noted previously, cus-
tomer backup data is encrypted before it is 
written to storage media. Therefore, even in 
the most unlikely event that a storage de-
vice is stolen from a processing facility, any 
data on the media remains inaccessible.

Leading SaaS data security |  18
Operational security measure
Explanation
Automation
The Keepit service is fully automated, operating based on the instructions (i.e., the configuration) provided by the 
customer. Therefore, no human operators outside of the customer’s own organization are involved in accessing, 
reviewing, or otherwise processing actual customer data. 
Restricted access
The Keepit platform itself is regularly updated as part of the ongoing maintenance and evolution of our service. 
However, there are no recurring or routine tasks that require human operators to access customer data. Furthermore, 
there are technical measures in place to ensure that no such access is required and that it is not easily or accidentally 
invoked. Additionally, there are organizational measures in place to educate and train staff on information security 
practices and policies. 
Regional support
If a customer needs assistance—and in the rare event that this assistance involves access to actual customer backup 
data—the Keepit support organization will work with the customer to ensure that such requests are served by support 
staff in an appropriate region, considering data sovereignty requirements, support availability, and time constraints. 
Third-party security assessments
Not only do we employ external auditors for security assessments, we also subject our platform to regular penetration 
testing conducted by third-party security and risk management specialists. This process replicates the tactics threat 
actors employ to gain Initial Access6, and extends beyond simple automated security scanners (which we also employ, 
of course). 
No subprocessors
Keepit has no subprocessors in connection with the provision of the Keepit Services. We adhere to the strictest data 
protection standards and ensure that no one else will be accessing or handling your data. This guarantees compliance 
with local regulations and that your data will always be handled with the highest level of sensitivity.

Physical operational health

Security features
In addition to the measures already pre-
sented (e.g., regional lock-in, dual data 
center redundancy), the Keepit platform 
also incorporates a number of additional 
security features to enhance protection of 
customer data. Two of the most important 
to govern are transport security and access 
control (Table 5).
Security feature
Explanation
TLS transport security
TLS transport security 
All primary workloads supported by Keepit employ modern Transport Layer Security (TLS) encryption on the endpoints used 
by Keepit and customers to access data. Both the Keepit Web UI and mobile app require the use of TLS. These communication 
protocols are designed to provide safe transport of data over insecure networks such as open Wi-Fi or broadband internet 
connections. 
 
Network security 
Additionally, to ensure a short path and the fastest possible data exchange with the primary customer data clouds for backup 
and restoration, Keepit connects directly to major internet exchanges. 
Secure and logged 
access controls
Single sign-on 
Keepit’s recommended best practice for deployment uses the customer’s existing authentication infrastructure (such as AD/
ADFS, Okta, etc.) by means of SAML integration. This approach allows customers to leverage the identity security measures they 
already have in place (e.g., multi-factor authentication). 
 
Fine-grained role-based access control 
Inside Keepit, an elaborate access control list (ACL) and role-based access control (RBAC) system allow fine-grained control 
over which identities can perform which operations on the customer tenant. For example, pre-defined policies permit an 
administrative role to manage the backup and a support role that can only restore data in place (as part of an internal IT support 
role) and cannot download or otherwise exfiltrate data from the platform. 
 
Additionally, separate groups of administrators can manage separate backup configurations; for example, one group can 
manage the Salesforce or Dynamics 365 backup while another manages the Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace 
backup. 
 
Immutable system audit log 
Finally, an audit trail is maintained for the duration of the customer engagement. The audit log can be viewed directly in the web 
application by authorized administrators and it can be accessed via the API for integration into third-party log analysis solutions. 
Data can also be pushed to Splunk, Sentinel or other third-party SIEM systems.

Conclusions
With increasing numbers of business- 
critical SaaS applications migrating to the 
cloud, and in a world in which new threats 
arise daily, continuity planning demands 
a secure SaaS data backup solution—and 
the SaaS vendors are clear that backups 
are your responsibility, not theirs.
The question then becomes: where to 
back up this critical data?
Keepit believes that real backup requires 
a separate logical infrastructure from the 
cloud in which the primary data is hosted. 
The most practical solution, then, is a dedi-
cated cloud platform.
But simply having a dedicated platform is 
not enough: the platform must be secure. 
However, security is not something that 
can be bolted on as an afterthought—it 
needs to be designed into the very es-
sence of a system. This secure-by-design 
philosophy guided the creation of The 
Keepit Cloud, which was architected from 
the ground up by information security and 
hosting experts to provide secure backup 
of SaaS data:
•	 Resilience and data immutability are achieved 
through immediate encryption of backup 
data, 30-day delete retention, data region 
sovereignty and dual data center redundancy, 
and a unique, tamper-proof infrastructure with 
immutability by default
•	 A blockchain-like Merkle tree architecture and 
innovative “incremental forever” data transfer 
ensure secure, reliable, and change-based 
long-term data storage
•	 All data center facilities employed by Keepit 
conform to a high physical security baseline 
and hold ISO 27001 certification plus comple-
mentary certifications (e.g., SOC-2, ISAE 3402, 
PCI/DSS, HIPAA)
•	 Technical and organizational measures are in 
place to ensure operational security, including 
a high degree of automation, comprehensive 
staff training, third-party security audits, 
proactive penetration testing, and detailed 
operational monitoring of the health of physical 
infrastructure and the software stack
•	 Mature software development lifecycle pro-
cesses ensure that security is incorporated 
from the inception of a new project and contin-
ued throughout the entire life of the system
•	 To enhance protection of customer data, the 
Keepit platform incorporates TLS transport

These characteristics and others combine 
to form a SaaS data backup solution that

Navigating NIS2: 
Essential cybersecurity measures
and compliance strategies
NIS2 Directive
The NIS2 Directive, set to be enacted into local 
law by October 17, 2024, implements the most 
comprehensive cybersecurity regulation in global 
history. It aims to bolster Europe’s defense against 
cyber threats by standardizing cybersecurity 
measures across the EU, particularly for 
organizations with critical infrastructure.
The NIS2 Directive imposes key obligations to 
enhance cybersecurity within the EU. Senior 
management must take responsibility for 
cybersecurity, including risk exposure and risk 
appetite. Organizations need to ensure their 
supply chains have appropriate security measures 
and implement clear incident handling and 
reporting procedures.
What’s new with NIS2?
•	 Broader scope of industries under regulation.
•	 Managing directors are personally liable.
•	 More stringent supervision and regulatory audits.
•	 Penalties can go up to 2% of global turnover.
Understanding your NIS2 responsibilities
Management responsibility
Supply chain security
Incident handling
Continuity and disaster recovery

measures such as disaster

What does a winning  
NIS2 strategy look like? 
 
To get your business ready for the regulation, the first step is to run a risk assessment to analyze 
which of your processes and data is critical to protect in order to ensure business continuity. 
Once you’ve done so, developing and regularly testing business continuity and disaster 
recovery plans is essential for compliance.
1.	 Map critical processes  
Assess and analyze critical business processes, 
as well as the digital assets and systems 
supporting them, to ensure business continuity.
2.	 Prioritize  
Identify crucial data, how to protect it and 
prioritize what to recover first in the event 
of an attack to minimize downtime.
3.	 Test that it works 
Frequently test that your contingency plans 
and backups work to instill confidence in 
your disaster recovery plan and promptly 
address any identified issues.
4.	 Document and analyze results  
After each testing session, document and 
analyze the time, accuracy and challenges 
encountered to gain insights for improvement.
5.	 Update and improve 
Continuously update recovery plans based on 
testing insights, addressing weaknesses, refining 
procedures, and adapting to evolving threats.

Financial institutions operate in a highly regulated environment, with SEC and FINRA rules 
requiring strict data retention, integrity, and accessibility practices. Regulations such as 
SEC Rule 17a-4 and FINRA recordkeeping requirements set the framework for how financial 
institutions manage and store critical records.
Keepit is designed to help organizations strengthen their data management practices by 
providing secure storage, audit-ready archiving, and streamlined access to records. Our 
solution offers features that support efforts to meet regulatory obligations while maintaining 
operational efficiency. Below, we outline key regulatory considerations and how Keepit can 
assist in addressing them. We will dive into the SEC Rule 17a-4 section first, before turning our 
attention to the FINRA requirements on the following page.

The integrity of backups is fundamental for recovery when data is lost and needs to be restored. 
But even without a data loss incident, documenting backup activities is now a key requirement 
for compliance and regulatory purposes.  With the growing adoption of SaaS applications and 
increasing regulatory pressure, having a single platform to support multi-SaaS environments 
becomes a game changer. 
As a cloud-native platform purposefully built for SaaS data protection, Keepit offers a set 
of observability, analytics, insights, and reporting capabilities that ensure the health and 
integrity of backups, identify potential risks to data, and provide a single pane of glass for SaaS 
backup and recovery activities. It saves time, reduces complexity, and simplifies reporting and 
compliance.
In this factsheet, you’ll find how our capabilities support observability and intelligent insights. 
We’ll walk you through common challenges you might encounter in this context and describe 
how Keepit can solve these challenges in a more intelligent way.
Observability and 
intelligent insights 
with Keepit
With growing coverage of critical SaaS applications, the Keepit platform offers centralized visibility and 
transparency over backup and recovery activities to functional managers and their teams. Expanding 
beyond the traditional coverage of Microsoft 365 and Salesforce, Keepit also offers backup and recovery 
services for Microsoft Entra ID, Power Platform, Jira and many more. We are continuously adding new

The ROI of ransomware recovery
Understanding the return on investment (ROI) for 
ransomware recovery is essential for businesses.
Total Economic Impact
In 2024, Keepit commissioned a Total Economic 
Impact (TM) study by Forrester Consulting which 
revealed significant findings. 
Based on interviews with Keepit customers, 
Forrester created a three-year financial model to 
determine the financial benefit of using Keepit to 
protect data in SaaS workloads. The study shows 
that Keepit’s solution offered a 163% ROI over three 
years, with a net present value of over $800,000. 
This demonstrates the substantial economic 
benefits that can be achieved through strategic 
investments in ransomware recovery capabilities.
Key statistics
•	
The Forrester TEI study revealed that Keepit’s 
solution provided a return on investment 
(ROI) of 163% over three years.
•	
Net present value of over $800,000: The same 
TEI study indicated that the net present value 
of Keepit’s solution was over $800,000.
•	
90% reduction in recovery time: Customers 
using Keepit’s solution reported a 90% 
reduction in the time needed for targeted 
restores after ransomware attacks.
•	
Payback within 6 months: Through its various 
benefits, the Keepit solution was shown to have 
a payback period of less than 6 months.
This is especially important as Forrester found a concerning gap when it comes to disaster recovery plans 
for SaaS platforms, per their research on the state of disaster recovery preparedness in the market.
Speaking on our recent webinar, Forrester senior analyst Brent Ellis said:
“[Out of 2000 enterprise software decision makers], 87% said they’re either currently using a SaaS 
application, or they plan to in the next 12 months. But [in a separate survey when I asked disaster recovery 
professionals] if SaaS platforms are within the scope of their organization’s disaster recovery planning, 
only 36% had a wholehearted yes. And when I asked does your organization currently backup your SaaS 
hosted data? 14% said no. And if you’re talking about disaster recovery planning and 14% don’t do 
backup of that data, that leaves a big question mark about whether you’re actually able to recover from a 
particular disaster to that platform.”

- Forrester’s Software 1 Survey, 2023

To enhance resilience against ransomware 
and other cyberthreats, organizations should 
implement several key strategies. First, conducting 
formal risk assessments is essential to identify 
critical infrastructure and data assets. Based 
on these assessments, businesses can develop 
prioritized disaster recovery plans tailored to their 
specific needs and vulnerabilities.
Additionally, ensuring that data backups are 
immutable and tamper proof is crucial. Regular 
testing and verification of backup integrity can 
prevent data loss and facilitate quick recovery 
in case of an attack. Finally, maintaining strong 
contracts with SaaS vendors is vital to ensure 
organizational resilience and security requirements 
are met.
These contracts should clearly define the vendor’s 
responsibilities and the security measures taken to 
protect data.
Strategies for enhancing resilience 
Risk factors for SaaS data 
resilience and disaster recovery
1. Shared platform vulnerabilities
•	
Dependency on shared infrastructure increases risk exposure.
•	
Potential for simultaneous failure of multiple systems. 
2. Exfiltration threats
•	
Unauthorized data access and transfer by cybercriminals.
•	
Risk of sensitive data being stolen or leaked.
 
3. Cyberattacks
•	
Ransomware targeting SaaS platforms.
•	
API exploits used to gain unauthorized access.
 
4. Limited version retention
•	
Inability to recover older versions of data.
•	
Increased risk of data loss due to limited backup versions.
 
5. Malicious data changes
•	
Intentional alterations to data by internal or external actors.
•	
Difficulty in detecting and reversing malicious modifications.
 
6. Accidental data changes
•	
Unintentional data deletions or modifications by users.
•	
Potential for significant operational disruption.
 
7. Role-based access control (RBAC) issues
•	
Excessive privileges granted to users.
•	
Increased risk of unauthorized data access and changes.
 
8. Platform misconfigurations
•	
Errors in configuring SaaS platforms.
•	
Increased vulnerability to cyberattacks and data breaches.
 
9. API exploits
•	
Attackers leveraging API vulnerabilities to access data.
•	
Risk of data manipulation and unauthorized actions.
 
10. Vendor dependency
•	
Reliance on SaaS vendors for data protection.
•	
Potential risks if the vendor’s security measures are inadequate.
 
11. Insufficient backup solutions
•	
Lack of comprehensive backup and recovery plans.
•	
Risk of extended downtime and data loss in disaster scenarios.
 
12. Compliance and regulatory risks
•	
Failure to meet data protection and privacy regulations.
•	
Potential for legal and financial penalties.
It’s vital for organizations to assess and analyze risk profiles for SaaS platforms in use, keeping these risk 
factors in mind, and understand how this affects their overall resilience. Based on these assessments, 
businesses can develop prioritized disaster recovery plans.

Hybrid warfare, nation-state attacks, and increasing 
cyber risk — how resilient is your organization?
As the line between physical and digital conflict blurs, CISOs and IT 
leaders face mounting pressure to protect critical infrastructure from 
sophisticated and ever-evolving threats. In a rapidly shifting threat 
landscape where cybercrime, system failures, and hybrid attacks are 
increasing in scale, sophistication, and impact, resilience becomes 
paramount. As global dependencies deepen, even small disruptions can 
have cascading consequences.  
This was the key focus of a recent Keepit webinar, where Kim Larsen, CISO 
at Keepit, and Ken Bonefeld Nielsen, Senior Cyber Security and Resilience 
Advisor at Norlys, explored how true resilience requires preparation, 
prioritization, and the ability to recover fast when the unexpected happens. 
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved.
Key takeaways
The threat landscape: What to consider
Cybercriminals are more capable than ever — now 
supported by powerful AI — and organizations must 
be prepared to deal with state actors, supply chain 
risks, and accidental outages. The world is deeply 
interconnected, meaning local disruptions trigger 
global consequences. 
Mission-critical systems and data must be 
identified, classified, and protected first. Trying 
to defend every asset equally leads to wasted 
resources and slow recovery, becoming a threat to 
business continuity.
Nations and organizations are being disrupted 
without formal declarations of war. Hybrid attacks 
combine cyber, physical, economic, and informa-
tion domains to create maximum impact. Resilience 
starts with mental resilience: understanding the 
threat and the scenarios to prepare for.
Absolute prevention is impossible. The true resil-
ience test is how fast you can restore operations 
when you’re under attack. Immutable backups, 
clear RPO/RTO objectives, and tested recovery 
plans are essential.
The threat landscape is 
changing rapidly
You can’t protect everything 
— prioritize what matters most
Hybrid attacks blur the line 
between peace and conflict
Recovery is as important 
as defense

AI’s promise is real — but today’s gains are mostly 
speed and task-level augmentation.
The organizations that will benefit are the ones that start with a clear 
business outcome and keep tight control of data and systems as 
they innovate. As agentic and LLM (large language models) tools knit 
applications together, traditional permission boundaries blur, attack 
volume and sophistication rise, and shadow IT accelerates. This means 
governance, security guardrails, and human-directed oversight are non-
negotiable.
This was the key focus of a recent Keepit webinar, where an expert panel 
led by Kim Larsen, CISO at Keepit, discussed how resilient data protection 
is the foundation for safe progress in AI. Immutable, sovereign backups 
with open, predictable access for analysis and precise recovery when 
things go wrong enable organizations to safely experiment.
© 2025 Keepit. All rights reserved.
Key takeaways
Where AI is today and where it is going
Productivity boosters (assistants, grammar, code 
acceleration). Helpful but not truly “intelligent”; 
limited novelty, mostly faster execution.
Agentic systems making decisions, orchestrating 
across apps and data. This changes the engineering 
model from procedural steps to event-driven, 
outcome-driven operations.
	
What this means
With agentic AI, the security landscape shifts 
dramatically: Familiar attacks like phishing, fraud, 
and impersonation scale to massive volumes and 
become more convincing, while new vectors 
emerge through model jailbreaks — sometimes 
hidden in text or even images — along with remote 
manipulation of agent behavior and a stronger 
focus on data exfiltration over encryption.
At the same time, traditional control points erode 
as small agents link systems together, weakening 
predefined permissions unless organizations 
introduce brokers or overseers to enforce 
constraints and maintain security.
As AI systems act more autonomously, governance 
and control become more important, not less. 
Organizations must codify what “good” looks like 
and enforce it. 
Where AI is today 
Where AI is going 
Secure by design 
Rethinking data protection in the AI era
Read our latest blog post: AI today - Power, 
drift, and the discipline to stay in control --→

Download now
Read our data governance report for more insight into how to best classify, 
protect, and recover your data so you can ensure operational continuity.
Intelligent data governance
Data protection’s evolving role
As systems grow more interdependent, data 
protection must evolve from simple point-in-time 
snapshots to restoring an entire coherent state. 
Achieving AI resilience requires immutability by 
design — so no agent or privileged user can tamper 
with backups — alongside vendor-independent 
storage that keeps data where policy dictates. 
Open, cost-predictable access to the platform is 
essential for safe analytics and training, supported 
by anomaly detection and time-machine history 
to distinguish “good” from compromised objects. 
Recovery must also become more precise, with 
guided, fine-grained restores that roll back only 
what’s necessary.
To stay resilient, organizations must demand 
immutability, sovereignty, anomaly detection, 
and granular recovery from their data-protection 
vendors. Ultimately, winning with AI isn’t about 
adopting it everywhere, but about maintaining 
control. The companies that define outcomes, 
enforce guardrails, and ensure recoverability will 
be best positioned to innovate boldly, absorb 
missteps, and bounce back fast.
Keep an eye out for these emerging offerings…
•	
Cross-workload intelligence. Unifying SaaS 
silos in a single immutable platform enables 
anomaly detection, discovery, and selective 
access for model training. 
•	
Guided recovery. Conversational restore 
assistants that leverage detailed data-change 
history to minimize user effort in complex 
incidents (e.g., restoring only the 5% of 
documents altered by ransomware across 
1,000 users). 
How to successfully adopt AI capabilities 
Successful AI adoption follows a simple framework: Start with the outcome by defining the decision or 
process to improve, along with clear success metrics and acceptable risk; establish controls through 
policies and technical guardrails such as data boundaries, model scope, agent conditions, auditability, and 
rollback paths; and finally, drive enablement by providing approved tools, patterns, and sandboxes that 
meet compliance and sovereignty needs, allowing teams to innovate safely and at speed.
Enablement
Controls
Outcome

4. How Keepit Counts Seats  
 
 
Count as Seat 
Microsoft 
365 
Exchange 
OneDrive 
SharePoint 
Groups/Teams 
To be counted as a seat the following must apply:  
• 
The user or item must be selected for backup in the relevant 
configuration directly or indirectly (such as group-based SharePoint site 
members).  
• 
The user or item must be active and have an assigned relevant Microsoft 
Office 365 license with an appropriate plan enabled. 
Depending on the license types, a Full, Light, Faculty, or Student seat is 
assigned. For example:  
• 
Microsoft license types E1, E2, E3, and E5 are counted as Full seats. 
• 
Microsoft license types F1, F3 and F5 are counted as Light seats. 
• 
Microsoft license types E1, E3, E5 for Faculty, and A1, A3 and A5 for 
Faculty are counted as Faculty seats.  
• 
Microsoft license types E1, E3, E5 for Students, and A1, A3 and A5 for 
Students are counted as Student seats 
The full list of Microsoft licenses and the classification can be found in the 
Keepit Knowledge Base. 
The total number of seats are calculated based on the M365 application with 
the highest number of users and items within the measuring period1.

5. Terms And Termination 
a. Retention 
Customers with an active subscription can choose the retention length of their backup (ranging from 12 
months to unlimited retention).  
b. Data Processing 
Keepit shall process personal data on behalf of the Customer in accordance with the Customer’s instruction. 
For detailed information, please refer to Keepit’s Data Processing Agreement: https://www.keepit.com/data-
processing-agreement/  
c. Exceeding Agreed Usage  
If customers and partners exceed the number of seats specified in their current agreement, they will receive 
an email from the Keepit Customer Success team. From the receipt of the email, they have 30 days to reduce 
the number of seats to fit the entitlement specified in their current agreement.     
If customers or partners do not reduce the number of seats to the entitled amount based on their current 
agreement, the Customer Success team will update their subscription to the new number of seats. The new 
seat count will include the exceeding seats from the month following when the exceeded usage was identified. 
If, as a partner, you have set a hard seat limit in your customer's custom properties and the number is 
exceeded, you will have 30 days to adjust the customer's product configuration accordingly. You can do so 
within your Partner Management Console. Read more about how to manage custom properties here.

Severity Level Definitions 
Level 
Definition 
Urgent  
Critical Business Impact 
 
A problem or issue has occurred where no workaround is immediately available in one of the 
following situations: (i) a production server or other mission critical system is down or has had a 
substantial loss of service; or (ii) mission critical data is at a significant risk of loss or corruption; 
or (iii) login entry system is not working. 
High  
Severe Business Impact 
A problem or issue has occurred where a major function is severely impaired. Operations can 
continue in a restricted fashion, although long-term productivity might be adversely affected. 
For example, it is not possible to download data as .PST. 
Medium 
Limited Business Impact 
A problem or issue has occurred with a limited adverse effect on business operations. For 
example, password protected links do not work. 
Low 
Minor Business Impact 
A problem or issue where business operations have not been adversely affected. For example, 
User Interface issues which have no impact on performance.
